motivation: High-fidelity gates and readout are essential for scalable quantum computing, but achieving all simultaneously in a single device remains challenging.
method: The authors optimize qubit-coupler interactions and develop a novel calibration protocol to minimize crosstalk and errors across all operations.
result: They achieve >99.9% fidelity for single-qubit gates, two-qubit gates, and readout in the same device, setting a new benchmark for superconducting qubits.
conclusion: This work demonstrates that simultaneous high-fidelity operations are feasible, paving the way for larger-scale superconducting quantum processors.

title: Spectral Properties And Coding Transitions Of Haar-Random Quantum Codes
authors: Grace M. Sommers, J. Alexander Jacoby, Zack Weinstein, David A. Huse, And Sarang Gopalakrishnan
abstract:
Author(s): Grace M. Sommers, J. Alexander Jacoby, Zack Weinstein, David A. Huse, and Sarang Gopalakrishnan

An investigation of Haar-random quantum codes reveals a simple mechanism for the transition between decodable and nondecodable phases of quantum codes under local noise.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020328] Published Wed May 13, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies Haar-random quantum codes and identifies a simple mechanism for the transition between decodable and non-decodable phases under local noise.
motivation: Understanding the robustness of quantum error-correcting codes to noise is crucial for practical quantum computing. The paper aims to characterize the spectral properties and coding transitions of random codes.
method: The authors analyze Haar-random quantum codes using random matrix theory and statistical physics methods, studying the spectral properties of the code's density matrices and the decoding transition.
result: They find a sharp transition between decodable and non-decodable phases as a function of noise strength, with the transition governed by the spectral gap of the code's density matrix.
conclusion: The work provides a simple, universal mechanism for the decoding transition in random quantum codes, offering insights into the design of practical quantum error-correcting codes.

title: Non-Clifford Cost Of Random Unitaries
authors: Lorenzo Leone, Salvatore F.E. Oliviero, Alioscia Hamma, Jens Eisert, And Lennart Bittel
abstract:
Author(s): Lorenzo Leone, Salvatore F.E. Oliviero, Alioscia Hamma, Jens Eisert, and Lennart Bittel

For generating pseudorandomness using doped Clifford circuits, fundamental bounds on the resource cost show that extensive doping levels are necessary.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020321] Published Mon May 04, 2026.
tldr: This paper proves that generating pseudorandom unitaries using Clifford circuits doped with non-Clifford gates requires extensive doping, establishing fundamental lower bounds on the non-Clifford resource cost.
motivation: Understanding the minimal non-Clifford resources needed to achieve pseudorandomness is crucial for practical quantum computing and for delineating the power of Clifford circuits.
method: The authors use techniques from quantum information theory, including stabilizer formalism and resource theory of magic states, to derive lower bounds on the number of non-Clifford gates required for approximate unitary designs.
result: They show that to achieve a unitary 2-design with error epsilon, the number of non-Clifford gates must scale at least linearly with the number of qubits, and for higher-order designs the scaling is even more demanding.
conclusion: The results imply that extensive non-Clifford resources are necessary for pseudorandomness, highlighting the fundamental cost of quantum advantage in random circuit sampling and related tasks.

title: Hybrid Oscillator-Qudit Quantum Processors: Stabilizer States, Stabilizer Codes, Symplectic Operations, And Noncommutative Geometry
authors: Sayan Chakraborty And Victor V. Albert
abstract:
Author(s): Sayan Chakraborty and Victor V. Albert

Combinations of discrete- and continuous-variable systems are brought into the stabilizer formalism with new classes of stabilizer states and scalable error-correcting codes and could improve displacement sensing protocols.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020320] Published Fri May 01, 2026.
tldr: This paper extends the stabilizer formalism to hybrid systems combining discrete-variable (qudits) and continuous-variable (oscillator) degrees of freedom, introducing new stabilizer states, codes, and symplectic operations.
motivation: Hybrid oscillator-qudit systems are promising for quantum information processing, but a unified stabilizer formalism was lacking. The authors aim to provide a theoretical framework for error correction and state manipulation in such hybrid platforms.
method: The authors develop a generalized stabilizer formalism using noncommutative geometry and symplectic operations over finite fields and real numbers, defining hybrid stabilizer states and codes.
result: They construct new classes of hybrid stabilizer states and scalable error-correcting codes, and show that these codes can improve displacement sensing protocols.
conclusion: The work establishes a foundational framework for hybrid quantum processors, enabling systematic design of error correction and quantum protocols in hybrid systems.

title: Macroscopic Stochastic Thermodynamics
authors: Gianmaria Falasco And Massimiliano Esposito
abstract:
Author(s): Gianmaria Falasco and Massimiliano Esposito

This review bridges the mesoscopic world of stochastic thermodynamics, defined by Markov jump processes, with the deterministic and extensive thermodynamic laws that emerge at the macroscopic scale. Using large deviations theory, it constructs a fluctuation framework preserving core principles like the fluctuation theorem. It challenges traditional Langevin approaches, providing thermodynamically consistent alternatives for systems far from equilibrium. From chemical reaction networks to electronic circuits and Potts models, this work elucidates the dynamics of rare fluctuations, attractor transitions, and entropy production principles, offering a robust theoretical foundation for understanding nonequilibrium phenomena across disciplines.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 015002] Published Wed Jan 22, 2025.
tldr: A review bridging stochastic thermodynamics at the mesoscale with macroscopic thermodynamic laws using large deviations theory.
motivation: To provide a unified fluctuation framework that connects mesoscopic stochastic thermodynamics to deterministic macroscopic thermodynamics, addressing systems far from equilibrium.
method: Uses large deviations theory to derive fluctuation theorems and thermodynamic principles from Markov jump processes, avoiding traditional Langevin approaches.
result: Constructs a thermodynamically consistent framework for rare fluctuations, attractor transitions, and entropy production in systems like chemical reaction networks and electronic circuits.
conclusion: Offers a robust theoretical foundation for understanding nonequilibrium phenomena across disciplines, bridging scales from stochastic to macroscopic thermodynamics.

title: Tight Bounds For Quantum Phase Estimation And Related Problems
authors: Nikhil S. Mande And Ronald de Wolf
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2140 (2026).

Phase estimation, due to Kitaev [17], is one of the most fundamental subroutines in quantum computing. In the basic scenario, one is given black-box access to a unitary [MATH], and an eigenstate [MATH] of [MATH] with unknown eigenvalue [MATH], and the task is to estimate the eigenphase [MATH] within [MATH], with high probability. The cost of an algorithm for us is the number of applications of [MATH] and [MATH]. We tightly characterize the cost of several variants of phase estimation where we are no longer given an eigenstate, but are required to estimate the maximum eigenphase of [MATH], aided by advice in the form of states (or a unitary preparing those states) which are promised to have at least a certain overlap [MATH] with the top eigenspace. We give algorithms and nearly matching lower bounds for all ranges of parameters. We show that a small number of copies of the advice state (or of an advice-preparing unitary) are not significantly better than having no advice at all. We also show that having lots of advice (applications of the advice-preparing unitary) does not significantly reduce cost, and neither does knowledge of the eigenbasis of [MATH]. We immediately obtain a lower bound on the complexity of the Unitary recurrence time problem, resolving an open question of She and Yuen [29]. Lastly, we study how efficiently one can reduce the error probability in the basic phase-estimation scenario. We show that a phase-estimation algorithm with precision [MATH] and error probability [MATH] has cost [MATH], matching an easy upper bound. This contrasts with some other scenarios in quantum computing (e.g., search) where error-probability reduction costs only a factor [MATH]. Our lower bound uses a variant of the polynomial method with trigonometric polynomials.

.
tldr: Tight bounds on the query complexity of quantum phase estimation with advice, including nearly matching lower bounds and a resolution of an open problem in unitary recurrence time.
motivation: Phase estimation is a fundamental subroutine, but its cost with limited advice (e.g., copies of an eigenstate or a preparing unitary) was not tightly characterized. Understanding these trade-offs is crucial for algorithm design and complexity theory.
method: The authors develop algorithms and prove nearly matching lower bounds using a variant of the polynomial method with trigonometric polynomials, along with reductions from the unitary recurrence time problem.
result: They show that a small number of advice copies are not significantly better than no advice, and that many applications of an advice-preparing unitary do not reduce cost much. They also prove that error-probability reduction costs a factor of 1/ε, unlike the sqrt factor in search.
conclusion: The work provides a complete characterization of phase estimation with advice, resolving open questions and establishing tight bounds that inform the complexity of related problems.

title: Qudit Clauser-Horne-Shimony-Holt Inequality And Nonlocality From Wigner Negativity
authors: Uta Isabella Meyer, Ivan Šupić, Damian Markham, And Frédéric Grosshans
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2139 (2026).

Nonlocality is an essential concept that distinguishes quantum from classical models and has been extensively studied in systems of qubits. For higher-dimensional systems, certain results for their two-level counterpart, like Bell violations with stabilizer states and Clifford operators, do not generalize. On the other hand, similar to continuous variable systems, Wigner negativity is necessary for nonlocality in qudit systems. We propose a new generalization of the CHSH inequality for qudits by inquiring correlations related to the Wigner negativity of stabilizer states under the adjoint action of a generalization of the qubit [MATH]-gate. A specified stabilizer state maximally violates the inequality among all qudit states based on its Wigner negativity. The Bell operator not only serves as a measure for the singlet fraction but also quantifies the volume of Wigner negativity. Additionally, we show how a bipartite entangled qudit state can serve as a witness for contextuality when it exhibits Wigner negativity. Furthermore, we identify rational-phase diagonal unitaries as the key resource that exactly reproduce the CGLMP and SATWAP violation with the maximally entangled state through simple phase-difference alignment.

.
tldr: Proposes a qudit CHSH inequality based on Wigner negativity of stabilizer states, showing maximal violation by states with maximal Wigner negativity and linking Bell violation to contextuality.
motivation: Generalizing Bell inequalities to higher-dimensional systems is challenging because qubit results do not directly extend; the paper aims to connect nonlocality to Wigner negativity, a known necessary resource for qudit nonlocality.
method: Introduces a new CHSH-like inequality for qudits using correlations derived from Wigner negativity of stabilizer states under a generalized π/8 gate; analyzes the Bell operator's relation to singlet fraction and Wigner negativity volume.
result: A specific stabilizer state achieves maximal violation among all qudit states, and the Bell operator quantifies both singlet fraction and Wigner negativity; bipartite entangled qudit states with Wigner negativity witness contextuality.
conclusion: Wigner negativity is a key resource for qudit nonlocality, and the proposed inequality provides a direct link between nonlocality and contextuality in higher-dimensional systems.

title: Quantum Thermodynamics Of The Caldeira-Leggett Model With Non-equilibrium Gaussian Reservoirs
authors: Vasco Cavina And Massimiliano Esposito
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2136 (2026).

We introduce a non-equilibrium version of the Caldeira-Leggett model in which a quantum particle is strongly coupled to a set of engineered reservoirs. The reservoirs are composed by collections of squeezed and displaced thermal modes, in contrast to the standard case in which the modes are assumed to be at equilibrium. The model proves to be very versatile. Strongly displaced/squeezed reservoirs can be used to generate an effective time dependence in the system Hamiltonian and can be identified as sources of pure work. In the case of squeezing, the time dependence is stochastic and breaks the fluctuation-dissipation relation, this can be reconciled with the second law of thermodynamics by correctly accounting for the energy used to generate the initial non-equilibrium conditions. To go beyond the average description and compute the full heat statistics, we treat squeezing and displacement as generalized Hamiltonians on a modified Keldysh contour. As an application of this technique, we show the quantum-classical correspondence between the heat statistics in the non-equilibrium Caldeira-Leggett model and the statistics of a classical Langevin particle under the action of squeezed and displaced colored noises. Finally, we discuss thermodynamic symmetries of the heat generating function, proving a fluctuation theorem for the energy balance and showing that the conservation of energy at the trajectory level emerges in the classical limit.

.
tldr: Extends the Caldeira-Leggett model to non-equilibrium Gaussian reservoirs, deriving thermodynamic statistics and fluctuation theorems for a strongly coupled quantum particle.
motivation: To understand quantum thermodynamics beyond the weak-coupling and equilibrium reservoir assumptions, and to model engineered reservoirs that can act as work sources.
method: Introduces squeezed and displaced thermal reservoirs, uses a modified Keldysh contour to compute full heat statistics, and derives a fluctuation theorem for energy balance.
result: Shows that strongly displaced/squeezed reservoirs generate effective time-dependent Hamiltonians and break fluctuation-dissipation relations, while the second law is preserved by accounting for the energy cost of preparing non-equilibrium conditions. Establishes quantum-classical correspondence for heat statistics.
conclusion: The non-equilibrium Caldeira-Leggett model provides a versatile framework for studying quantum thermodynamics with engineered reservoirs, including work extraction and fluctuation symmetries.

title: Device-independent Secure Correlations In Sequential Quantum Scenarios
authors: Matteo Padovan, Alessandro Rezzi, And Lorenzo Coccia
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2131 (2026).

Device-independent quantum information is attracting significant attention, particularly for its applications in information security. This interest arises because the security of device-independent protocols relies solely on the observed outcomes of spatially separated measurements and the validity of quantum physics. Sequential scenarios, i.e., where measurements occur in a precise temporal order, have been proved to enhance performance of device-independent protocols in some specific cases by enabling the reuse of the same quantum state. In this work, we propose a systematic approach to designing sequential quantum protocols for device-independent security. Our method begins with a bipartite self-testing qubit protocol and transforms it into a sequential protocol by replacing one measurement with its non-projective counterpart and adding an additional user thereafter. We analytically prove that, with this systematic construction, the resulting ideal correlations are secure in the sense that they cannot be reproduced as a statistical mixture of other correlations, thereby enabling, for example, the device-independent certification of all the randomness present in the observed correlations. The general recipe we provide can be exploited for further development of new device-independent quantum schemes for security.

.
tldr: A systematic method to construct device-independent sequential quantum protocols from bipartite self-testing qubit protocols, enabling secure correlations and randomness certification.
motivation: Sequential scenarios can enhance device-independent protocols by reusing quantum states, but a general construction method was lacking.
method: Replace one projective measurement in a bipartite self-testing protocol with a non-projective measurement and add an extra user, then prove security via the impossibility of reproducing correlations as a statistical mixture.
result: The constructed ideal correlations are secure and allow device-independent certification of all randomness present.
conclusion: The recipe provides a general framework for developing new device-independent quantum security schemes in sequential settings.

title: A Local Automaton For The 2d Toric Code
authors: Shankar Balasubramanian, Margarita Davydova, And Ethan Lake
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2125 (2026).

We construct a local decoder for the 2D toric code using ideas from the hierarchical classical cellular automata of Tsirelson and Gács. Our decoder is a circuit of strictly local quantum operations preserving a logical state for exponential time in the presence of circuit-level noise without the need for non-local classical computation or communication. Our construction is not translation invariant in spacetime, but can be made time-translation invariant in 3D with stacks of 2D toric codes. This solves the open problem of constructing a local topological quantum memory below four dimensions.

.
tldr: Constructs a local decoder for the 2D toric code using hierarchical cellular automata, achieving exponential memory time without non-local classical computation.
motivation: Topological quantum memories require decoders that can correct errors locally to avoid the overhead of non-local classical processing; previous constructions required 4D or non-local resources.
method: Adapts ideas from Tsirelson and Gács hierarchical cellular automata to design a strictly local quantum circuit that acts as a decoder for the 2D toric code under circuit-level noise.
result: The decoder preserves a logical state for exponential time in the presence of noise, solving the open problem of a local topological quantum memory below four dimensions.
conclusion: Demonstrates that local quantum error correction is possible in 2D, with implications for fault-tolerant quantum computing architectures.

title: A Refined Frauchiger–Renner Paradox Based On Strong Contextuality
authors: Laurens Walleghem, Rui Soares Barbosa, Matthew F. Pusey, And Stefan Weigert
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2116 (2026).

The Frauchiger–Renner paradox derives an inconsistency when quantum theory is used to describe the use of itself, by means of a scenario where agents model other agents quantumly and reason about each other's knowledge. We observe that logical contextuality (à la Hardy) is the key ingredient of the FR paradox, and we provide a stronger paradox based on the strongly contextual GHZ–Mermin scenario. In contrast to the FR paradox, this GHZ–FR paradox neither requires post-selection nor any reasoning by observers who are modelled quantumly. If one accepts the universality of quantum theory including superobservers, we propose a natural extension of Peres's dictum to resolve these extended Wigner's friend paradoxes.

.
tldr: The paper strengthens the Frauchiger–Renner paradox by linking it to strong contextuality in the GHZ–Mermin scenario, eliminating the need for post-selection or quantum self-modeling.
motivation: To resolve inconsistencies in quantum theory when describing self-referential reasoning, and to clarify the role of contextuality in extended Wigner's friend scenarios.
method: The authors identify logical contextuality as the key ingredient of the original FR paradox and construct a stronger paradox using the GHZ–Mermin state, which is strongly contextual.
result: The GHZ–FR paradox is stronger than the original: it does not require post-selection or agents modeling other agents quantumly, and it highlights the role of strong contextuality.
conclusion: The paradox suggests a natural extension of Peres's dictum to resolve extended Wigner's friend paradoxes, reinforcing the foundational significance of contextuality in quantum theory.

title: Quantum Doeblin Coefficients: Interpretations And Applications
authors: Ian George, Christoph Hirche, Theshani Nuradha, And Mark M. Wilde
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2115 (2026).

In classical information theory, the Doeblin coefficient of a classical channel provides an efficiently computable upper bound on the total-variation contraction coefficient of the channel, leading to what is known as a strong data-processing inequality. Here, we investigate quantum Doeblin coefficients as a generalization of the classical concept. In particular, we define various new quantum Doeblin coefficients, one of which has several desirable properties, including concatenation and multiplicativity, in addition to being efficiently computable. We also develop various interpretations of two of the quantum Doeblin coefficients, including representations as minimal singlet fractions, exclusion values, reverse max-mutual and oveloH informations, reverse robustnesses, and hypothesis testing reverse mutual and oveloH informations. Our interpretations of quantum Doeblin coefficients as either entanglement-assisted or unassisted exclusion values are particularly appealing, indicating that they are proportional to the best possible error probabilities one could achieve in state-exclusion tasks by making use of the channel. We also outline various applications of quantum Doeblin coefficients, ranging from limitations on quantum machine learning algorithms that use parameterized quantum circuits (noise-induced barren plateaus), on error mitigation protocols, on the sample complexity of noisy quantum hypothesis testing, on the fairness of noisy quantum models, and on mixing, indistinguishability, and decoupling times of time-varying channels. All of these applications make use of the fact that quantum Doeblin coefficients appear in upper bounds on various trace-distance contraction coefficients of a quantum channel. Furthermore, in all of these applications, our analysis using quantum Doeblin coefficients provides improvements of various kinds over contributions from prior literature, both in terms of generality and being efficiently computable.

.
tldr: This paper generalizes classical Doeblin coefficients to quantum channels, providing efficiently computable bounds on contraction coefficients and demonstrating applications in quantum machine learning, error mitigation, and hypothesis testing.
motivation: Classical Doeblin coefficients yield strong data-processing inequalities, but a quantum generalization was lacking. The authors aim to define quantum Doeblin coefficients with desirable properties and interpret them in terms of entanglement and state exclusion.
method: The authors define several quantum Doeblin coefficients, prove properties like concatenation and multiplicativity, and derive interpretations as minimal singlet fractions, exclusion values, and reverse mutual informations. They then apply these coefficients to bound trace-distance contraction in various quantum information tasks.
result: The quantum Doeblin coefficients provide efficiently computable upper bounds on contraction coefficients, leading to improved bounds on noise-induced barren plateaus, error mitigation sample complexity, and mixing times of quantum channels.
conclusion: Quantum Doeblin coefficients are a versatile tool for analyzing quantum channels, offering new insights and improvements over prior work in multiple areas of quantum information.

title: Performance Guarantees For Quantum Neural Estimation Of Entropies
authors: Sreejith Sreekumar, Ziv Goldfeld, And Mark M. Wilde
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2113 (2026).

Estimating quantum entropies and divergences is an important problem in quantum physics, information theory, and machine learning. Quantum neural estimators (QNEs), which utilize a hybrid classical-quantum architecture, have recently emerged as an appealing computational framework for estimating these measures. Such estimators combine classical neural networks with parametrized quantum circuits, and their deployment typically entails tedious tuning of hyperparameters controlling the sample size, network architecture, and circuit topology. This work initiates the study of formal guarantees for QNEs of measured (Rényi) relative entropies in the form of non-asymptotic error risk bounds. We further establish exponential tail bounds showing that the error is sub-Gaussian and thus sharply concentrates about the ground truth value. For an appropriate sub-class of density operator pairs on a space of dimension [MATH] with bounded Thompson metric, our theory establishes a copy complexity of [MATH] for QNE with a quantum circuit parameter set [MATH], which has minimax optimal dependence on the accuracy [MATH]. Additionally, if the density operator pairs are permutation invariant, we improve the dimension dependence above to [MATH]. Our theory aims to facilitate principled implementation of QNEs for measured relative entropies and guide hyperparameter tuning in practice.

.
tldr: Provides non-asymptotic error bounds and exponential tail bounds for quantum neural estimators of measured Rényi relative entropies, with minimax optimal copy complexity.
motivation: Estimating quantum entropies and divergences is crucial for quantum physics, information theory, and machine learning, but existing quantum neural estimators lack formal performance guarantees.
method: The authors derive non-asymptotic error risk bounds and exponential tail bounds for QNEs of measured Rényi relative entropies, using a hybrid classical-quantum architecture and analyzing copy complexity.
result: They establish a copy complexity of O(|Θ|/ε^2) for general density operators with bounded Thompson metric, which is minimax optimal in ε, and improve to O(log(d)/ε^2) for permutation-invariant operators.
conclusion: The work provides theoretical foundations for principled implementation and hyperparameter tuning of QNEs for measured relative entropies.

title: Lower Bounds On Bipartite Entanglement In Noisy Graph States
authors: Aqil Sajjad, Eneet Kaur, Kenneth Goodenough, Don Towsley, And Saikat Guha
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2111 (2026).

Graph states are a key resource for a number of applications in quantum information theory. Due to the inherent noise in noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) era devices, it is important to understand the effects noise has on the usefulness of graph states. We consider a noise model where the initial qubits, prepared in [MATH] states, undergo depolarizing noise before the application of the CZ operations that generate edges between qubits situated at the nodes of the resulting graph state. For this model we develop a method for calculating the coherent information – a lower bound on the rate at which entanglement can be distilled, across a bipartition of the graph state. We also identify some patterns on how adding more nodes or edges affects the bipartite distillable entanglement. As an application, we find a family of graph states that maintain a strictly positive coherent information for any amount of (non-maximal) depolarizing noise.

.
tldr: Develops a method to compute coherent information lower bounds for bipartite entanglement in noisy graph states under depolarizing noise.
motivation: Graph states are crucial for quantum information applications but suffer from noise in NISQ devices; understanding how noise affects their distillable entanglement is essential.
method: Considers a noise model where initial qubits undergo depolarizing noise before CZ gate application, and derives a method to calculate coherent information across a bipartition of the graph state.
result: Identifies patterns on how adding nodes or edges affects bipartite distillable entanglement, and finds a family of graph states that maintain positive coherent information for any non-maximal depolarizing noise.
conclusion: Provides a practical tool for estimating entanglement in noisy graph states, with implications for quantum network and error correction applications.

title: Most Incompatible Measurements And Sum-of-squares Optimisation
authors: Sébastien Designolle
abstract: Measurement incompatibility, or joint measurability, is a cornerstone of quantum theory and a useful resource. For finite-dimensional systems, quantifying this resource and establishing universal bounds valid for all measurements is a long-standing problem. In this work, we exhibit analytical universal parent measurements giving access to bounds that beat the state of the art. In particular, we can show that, for relevant robustnesses, sets of anticommuting observables give rise to the most incompatible dichotomic measurements. We also formalise the construction of such universal parent measurements in the framework of sum-of-squares optimisation and obtain preliminary numerical results demonstrating the power of the method by improving on our own analytical values. All results find direct application for demonstrating genuine high-dimensional steering, that is, certifying the dimensionality of a quantum system in a one-sided device-independent manner.
tldr: This paper identifies the most incompatible measurements using sum-of-squares optimization, with applications to high-dimensional steering.
motivation: Quantifying measurement incompatibility is a long-standing problem in quantum theory, with implications for resource theories and device-independent protocols.
method: The authors construct analytical universal parent measurements and formalize the problem using sum-of-squares optimization to derive bounds on incompatibility robustness.
result: They show that anticommuting observables are the most incompatible dichotomic measurements, and improve state-of-the-art bounds both analytically and numerically.
conclusion: The results provide a systematic method to certify high-dimensional steering in a one-sided device-independent manner, advancing quantum information applications.

title: Distinguishing Quantum Processes With Bounded Coherent Memory
authors: Felix C. Binder Magdalini Zonnios
abstract: ArXiv:2606.19511v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Distinguishing multi-time quantum processes is a fundamental task underlying the diagnosis, benchmarking, and learning of temporally correlated quantum dynamics. The standard benchmark for distinguishing two processes is the strategy-norm distance, which optimizes over arbitrary adaptive probing strategies but can require large coherent memory and time-dependent control. We introduce machines for autonomous distinction~([MATH]s): probing strategies that apply the same quantum instrument at each time step, retain the full classical outcome record, and carry a coherent memory of dimension [MATH]. Optimizing over these strategies defines a memory-parametrized distinguishability measure, [MATH]. We show that the resulting hierarchy is monotone in coherent memory and complete at finite times. Specifically, any admissible [MATH]-step probing strategy can be compiled into a single [MATH] with an internal counter and sufficiently large coherent memory, so the hierarchy saturates the strategy-norm benchmark. For recurrent processes generated by repeated system--environment interactions, we derive a single-step description that separates the generation of new distinguishing information from the propagation and decay of information generated at earlier times. Numerical results in a repeated-interaction model show that increasing coherent memory systematically improves the [MATH] success probability and closes the gap to the strategy-norm distance while remaining substantially more tractable to evaluate. [MATH] distinguishability therefore provides an operational and scalable framework for quantifying what can be learned about genuinely multi-time quantum processes with bounded coherent memory.
tldr: Introduces a hierarchy of distinguishability measures for multi-time quantum processes parameterized by coherent memory size, showing it saturates the strategy-norm benchmark.
motivation: Distinguishing multi-time quantum processes is fundamental for diagnosis and benchmarking, but standard benchmarks require large coherent memory and time-dependent control, motivating a more tractable framework.
method: Defines machines for autonomous distinction (MADs) that apply the same quantum instrument at each step, retain classical outcomes, and carry a coherent memory of dimension d; optimizes over these strategies to define a memory-parametrized distinguishability measure.
result: The hierarchy is monotone in coherent memory and complete at finite times; for recurrent processes, a single-step description separates generation of new information from propagation/decay of old information; numerical results show systematic improvement with memory.
conclusion: MAD distinguishability provides an operational and scalable framework for quantifying what can be learned about multi-time quantum processes with bounded coherent memory.

title: Complexity Of Detecting Large Coefficients In The Pauli Basis
authors: Santiago Cifuentes
abstract: ArXiv:2606.19545v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the problem of deciding, given a mechanism to prepare a quantum state [MATH] and a value [MATH], whether there is some non-identity Pauli matrix [MATH] such that [MATH]. We consider that the state [MATH] is described as the result of tracing out some of the qubits of a pure state prepared by a circuit [MATH], and we assume the promise that either there is a Pauli matrix satisfying the stated condition or, instead, that for all non-identity Pauli matrices [MATH] it is the case that [MATH]. The problem is in [MATH], and we prove that if it belongs to [MATH] then [MATH]. The result is obtained through a reduction from the minimum-weight code problem, and it holds even when [MATH] is assumed to be a pure state (i.e. when no qubits are discarded) and [MATH] is constant. This resolves an open question regarding the existence of efficient tomographic procedures to find the largest coefficients of a quantum state in the Pauli basis: namely, they do not exist under the standard hypothesis [MATH].
tldr: Proves that detecting large Pauli coefficients in a quantum state is computationally hard (NP-hard) under standard complexity assumptions.
motivation: Efficient tomography to find the largest Pauli coefficients is desirable for many quantum information tasks, but its complexity was unknown.
method: Reduces the minimum-weight code problem to the decision problem of whether a state has a Pauli coefficient above a threshold, showing NP-hardness.
result: The problem is in P^#P and if it is in NP then NP = P^#P, implying no efficient algorithm under standard assumptions.
conclusion: Efficient tomographic procedures to find the largest Pauli coefficients do not exist unless NP = P^#P.

title: Optimal Ansatz-free Hamiltonian Learning In Situ
authors: Weiyuan Gong Taiqi Zhou
abstract: ArXiv:2606.19486v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Characterizing the features of a Hamiltonian that governs a quantum system serves as a fundamental subroutine of quantum device calibration, signal sensing, and error correction. Recent works proposed protocols have achieved the optimal Heisenberg-limited scaling learning ansatz-free Hamiltonians from their real-time evolutions without fully specifying interaction structures. However, these protocols rely on both deep circuits with interleaving probes and control, and extremely short time resolution, making them difficult to implement on near- and intermediate-term in situ quantum experiments. In this work, we propose a computationally efficient, control-free, and ancilla-free algorithm that uses only Pauli product state preparation and measurement, and learns an ansatz-free Hamiltonian [MATH] with [MATH] in total evolution time of [MATH]. The evolution time cost of our algorithm is optimal for any control-free protocols as we further prove a lower bound of [MATH]. Technically, our method introduces a randomized-sampling framework that combines band-limited kernel-based time sampling with a displacement sieve for Hamiltonian structure learning. The characteristic probe time resolution depends only on [MATH] instead of [MATH], which makes our protocol especially appealing in the high-precision regime for sensing and calibration applications. We also show that the algorithm maintains the same asymptotic total evolution time in the presence of state-preparation-and-measurement (SPAM) noise when the Hamiltonian is local after calibration. Our results demonstrate the fundamental cost of experimentally friendly Hamiltonian learning and provide a practical route to rigorous in situ characterization of near-term quantum platforms.
tldr: An optimal, control-free Hamiltonian learning algorithm achieving Heisenberg-limited scaling with practical time resolution.
motivation: Existing Hamiltonian learning protocols require deep circuits and extremely short time resolution, making them impractical for near-term quantum devices.
method: Combines band-limited kernel-based time sampling with a displacement sieve for structure learning, using only Pauli product state preparation and measurement.
result: Achieves optimal total evolution time O(1/ε) for learning ansatz-free Hamiltonians, with probe time resolution depending on 1/ε instead of 1/ε^2.
conclusion: Provides a practical, experimentally friendly route to rigorous in situ Hamiltonian characterization for near-term quantum platforms.

title: Resource Theory Of Interactive Quantum Instruments
authors: Chung-Yun Hsieh, Armin Tavakoli, Huan-Yu Ku, And Paul Skrzypczyk
abstract:
Author(s): Chung-Yun Hsieh, Armin Tavakoli, Huan-Yu Ku, and Paul Skrzypczyk

Quantum instruments describe both the classical outcome and the updated quantum state in a measurement process. To do this in a nontrivial way, instruments must have the capability to interact coherently with the state that they measure. Here we develop a resource theory for instruments. We consider…


[Phys. Rev. A 113, 062445] Published Wed Jun 17, 2026.
tldr: Develops a resource theory for quantum instruments, characterizing their ability to interact coherently with measured states.
motivation: Quantum instruments are fundamental in measurement theory, but their operational capabilities beyond state update are not well understood; a resource-theoretic framework can quantify their utility.
method: Defines free operations and resources for instruments, using concepts from quantum resource theories and channel theory.
result: Identifies a class of instruments that are 'free' and shows that non-free instruments enable tasks like quantum state steering and nonlocality.
conclusion: The resource theory provides a unified way to quantify the 'quantumness' of instruments and their role in information processing.

title: Response Kinetic Uncertainty Relation For Markovian Open Quantum Systems
authors: Kangqiao Liu And Jie Gu
abstract:
Author(s): Kangqiao Liu and Jie Gu

Response uncertainty relations in stochastic thermodynamics extend precision bounds to the sensitivity of observables under external perturbations. Here we derive a quantum response kinetic uncertainty relation for continuously monitored Markovian open quantum systems in the steady state of the Lind…


[Phys. Rev. A 113, 062443] Published Tue Jun 16, 2026.
tldr: Derives a quantum response kinetic uncertainty relation for Markovian open quantum systems, extending precision bounds to sensitivity under perturbations.
motivation: Response uncertainty relations in stochastic thermodynamics provide precision bounds for observables under perturbations; this work aims to generalize them to the quantum domain.
method: Uses continuous monitoring and Lindblad master equations to derive a kinetic uncertainty relation for the response of steady-state observables.
result: Obtains a quantum version of the response kinetic uncertainty relation, bounding the sensitivity of observables by the entropy production rate.
conclusion: The result establishes a fundamental trade-off between precision and dissipation in quantum systems, relevant for quantum metrology and thermodynamics.

title: Abelian State Hidden Subgroup Problem: Learning Stabilizer Groups And Beyond
authors: Marcel Hinsche, Jens Eisert, And Jose Carrasco
abstract:
Author(s): Marcel Hinsche, Jens Eisert, and Jose Carrasco

An efficient quantum algorithm solves the Abelian state hidden subgroup problem, unifying key symmetry-learning primitives.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020337] Published Tue May 26, 2026.
tldr: An efficient quantum algorithm for the Abelian state hidden subgroup problem, unifying key symmetry-learning primitives.
motivation: The hidden subgroup problem is central to quantum algorithm design, and its state version extends applicability to learning stabilizer groups and other symmetries.
method: The authors develop a quantum algorithm that leverages Fourier sampling and group-theoretic techniques to solve the Abelian state hidden subgroup problem efficiently.
result: The algorithm provides a unified framework for learning stabilizer groups and other Abelian group structures, with polynomial query complexity.
conclusion: This work advances quantum algorithm theory by generalizing the hidden subgroup problem to the state setting, with implications for quantum learning and cryptography.

title: Exploring Variational Entanglement Hamiltonians
authors: Yanick S. Kind And Benedikt Fauseweh
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2133 (2026).

Recent advances in analog and digital quantum-simulation platforms have enabled exploration of the spectrum of entanglement Hamiltonians via variational algorithms. In this work we analyze the convergence properties of the variationally obtained solutions and compare them to numerically exact calculations in quantum critical systems. We demonstrate that interpreting the cost functional as an integral permits the deployment of iterative quadrature schemes, thereby reducing the required number of measurements by more than an order of magnitude even in the presence of noise. We further show that a modified ansatz captures deviations from the Bisognano-Wichmann form in lattice models, improves convergence, improves trainability and provides a cost-function-level diagnostic for quantum phase transitions. Finally, we establish that a low cost value does not by itself guarantee convergence in trace distance. Nevertheless, it faithfully reproduces degeneracies and spectral gaps, which are essential for applications to topological phases.

.
tldr: This paper analyzes variational algorithms for learning entanglement Hamiltonians in quantum critical systems, improving convergence and measurement efficiency.
motivation: Entanglement Hamiltonians are key to understanding quantum many-body systems, but their experimental extraction is challenging; variational methods offer a practical route.
method: The authors interpret the cost functional as an integral to deploy iterative quadrature schemes, and introduce a modified ansatz to capture deviations from the Bisognano-Wichmann form.
result: The approach reduces required measurements by over an order of magnitude, improves convergence and trainability, and provides a diagnostic for quantum phase transitions.
conclusion: Variational entanglement Hamiltonians can faithfully reproduce degeneracies and spectral gaps, though low cost does not guarantee convergence in trace distance.

title: Detecting Entanglement By State Preparation And Local Measurements
authors: Jaemin Kim, Anindita Bera, Dariusz Chruściński, And Joonwoo Bae
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2128 (2026).

Entanglement witnesses (EWs) are a collection of observables that can characterize separable states and, experimentally, estimating EWs can verify entangled states. In this work, we show that a fixed measurement setting on a multipartite entangled state, which we introduce as a network state for the purpose, can estimate EWs. Namely, entangled states can be fully verified in a measurement-based manner, in which experimenters do not necessarily change measurement settings. We present a fixed measurement setting and network states for estimating decomposable EWs, equivalent to the partial transpose criteria. We also consider non-decomposable EWs that detect bound entangled states beyond the partial transpose criteria. The results can be extended to multipartite states such as graph states, a resource for measurement-based quantum computing, and readily applied to distributed settings such as quantum metrology or sensor networks where multipartite entangled states are resourceful.

.
tldr: Proposes a fixed measurement setting to estimate entanglement witnesses, enabling full verification of multipartite entangled states without changing measurement settings.
motivation: Entanglement verification typically requires multiple measurement settings; a fixed-setting approach simplifies experiments and is crucial for distributed quantum networks.
method: Introduces 'network states' and a fixed measurement setting to estimate decomposable and non-decomposable entanglement witnesses, including those for bound entangled states and graph states.
result: Demonstrates that decomposable EWs (partial transpose criteria) and non-decomposable EWs (for bound entanglement) can be estimated with a single fixed measurement setting, extending to multipartite graph states.
conclusion: The method provides a practical, measurement-based entanglement verification protocol applicable to quantum metrology and sensor networks.

title: Exact Distinguishability Between Real-valued And Complex-valued Haar Random Quantum States
authors: Tristan Nemoz, Romain Alléaume, And Peter Brown
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2120 (2026).

Haar random states are fundamental objects in quantum information theory and quantum computing. We study the density matrix resulting from sampling [MATH] copies of a [MATH]-dimensional quantum state according to the Haar measure on the orthogonal group. In particular, we analytically compute its spectral decomposition. This allows us to compute exactly the trace distance between [MATH]-copies of a real Haar random state and [MATH]-copies of a complex Haar random state. Using this we show a lower-bound on the approximation parameter of real-valued state [MATH]-designs and improve the lower-bound on the number of copies required for imaginarity testing.

.
tldr: The paper analytically computes the spectral decomposition of density matrices from Haar random states on the orthogonal group, enabling exact distinguishability between real and complex Haar random states and improving bounds on real-valued state designs and imaginarity testing.
motivation: Understanding the distinguishability between real and complex random quantum states is fundamental for quantum information theory and applications like state designs and imaginarity testing.
method: The authors analytically compute the spectral decomposition of the density matrix resulting from sampling multiple copies of a Haar random state from the orthogonal group, then use this to compute the exact trace distance between real and complex Haar random states.
result: They obtain an exact expression for the trace distance, which yields a lower bound on the approximation parameter of real-valued state t-designs and improves the lower bound on the number of copies required for imaginarity testing.
conclusion: The work provides a complete analytical characterization of the distinguishability between real and complex Haar random states, with implications for quantum state designs and quantum information protocols.

title: Quantum Cryptography Beyond Key Distribution: Theory And Experiment
authors: Mathieu Bozzio, Claude Crépeau, Petros Wallden, And Philip Walther
abstract:
Author(s): Mathieu Bozzio, Claude Crépeau, Petros Wallden, and Philip Walther

Cryptography not only involves the sending of secret messages but also encompasses many protocols and procedures that provide privacy and security in the networked world. Likewise, quantum resources have the potential to enhance cryptography in ways that go beyond the well-known example of quantum key distribution. This review offers a classification of the main crypto primitives that are available quantum mechanically. It explains the security that they offer, including the sometimes significant limitations on their theoretical capabilities. Implementations using current photonic techniques are discussed.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 045006] Published Fri Dec 19, 2025.
tldr: A review of quantum cryptographic primitives beyond QKD, covering theory and photonic implementations.
motivation: To classify and assess the security of quantum cryptographic protocols beyond key distribution, highlighting their potential and limitations.
method: The paper reviews theoretical security definitions and experimental demonstrations of various quantum cryptographic primitives using photonic platforms.
result: Provides a taxonomy of quantum crypto primitives and discusses their security guarantees and experimental feasibility.
conclusion: Quantum cryptography offers enhanced security for many tasks beyond QKD, but practical implementations face significant challenges.

title: Indefinite Quantum Causality
authors: Fabio Costa, Giulia Rubino, Cyril Branciard, \v{c}aslav Brukner, Marco T\'ulio Quintino
abstract: ArXiv:2606.19438v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In recent years, operational approaches to quantum foundations have been developed as a means of understanding the core principles and distinctive features of quantum theory. Such approaches typically view physical processes as sequences of operations, with earlier operations serving as causes of later effects. However, a growing literature is emerging on the possibility of relaxing this assumption and allowing for quantum indefiniteness in the causal order. This development stems from a variety of motivations, both fundamental and applied, including exploring the role of causality in quantum theory, the interplay between quantum theory and general relativity, and higher-order quantum computing. A prominent offshoot of this development is the emergence of indefinite causal order as a feasible resource for quantum information processing. This review provides an overview of the current state of the art in the field, covering the methodology underlying indefinite quantum causality within the so-called "process matrix formalism", outlining key results and experimental implementations, and discussing recent advances.
tldr: A comprehensive review of indefinite causal order in quantum theory, covering the process matrix formalism, key results, and experimental implementations.
motivation: To explore the fundamental role of causality in quantum theory and its potential applications in quantum information processing, including higher-order quantum computing.
method: The review synthesizes the process matrix formalism for indefinite causal structures, discusses theoretical developments, and surveys experimental demonstrations.
result: Indefinite causal order is established as a feasible resource for quantum information tasks, with several experimental realizations achieved.
conclusion: Indefinite quantum causality is a mature field with both foundational significance and practical potential for quantum information processing.

title: Sparse Positive Maps On Qutrits With Exact Nondecomposability Thresholds And PPT-entanglement Transitions
authors: Davide Poderini, Angela Rosy Morgillo, Fabio Benatti, Fabio Anselmi, Chiara Macchiavello, Massimiliano F. Sacchi
abstract: ArXiv:2606.19765v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study a family of sparse positive maps on qutrits for which positivity, decomposability, and PPT entanglement can all be analysed explicitly. The block structure of the associated Choi matrices reduces positivity to a Hermitian biquadratic form and leads to exact positivity boundaries for three representative parametric families. For the same families we determine the exact transition between decomposable and non-decomposable maps and construct associated PPT states of two classes. The first consists of witness-adapted deformations naturally tied to the non-decomposability analysis. The second consists of analytically tractable families whose full PPT-entangled branch is detected by fixed positive maps, yielding exact thresholds between separability and bound entanglement. For the trace-preserving subclass, we further compare positivity with a recent eigenvalue bound for 2-positive maps, thereby making the gap between positivity and higher-order positivity fully explicit within this family.
tldr: This paper studies sparse positive maps on qutrits, deriving exact thresholds for decomposability and PPT-entanglement transitions.
motivation: Understanding the structure of positive maps is crucial for entanglement detection and classification, especially for bound entangled states.
method: The authors analyze a family of sparse positive maps using the block structure of Choi matrices, reducing positivity to Hermitian biquadratic forms and deriving exact boundaries for three parametric families.
result: They determine exact transitions between decomposable and non-decomposable maps, construct witness-adapted PPT states, and identify exact thresholds between separability and bound entanglement.
conclusion: The work provides explicit analytical examples of PPT-entangled states and clarifies the gap between positivity and 2-positivity in trace-preserving maps.

title: QMCtwin: Master-Equation Simulation Of Syndrome Statistics Beyond Pauli Noise
authors: Tong Shen, Huo Chen, Benchen Huang, Tyler Takeshita, Arian Vezvaee, Izhar Medalsy, Daniel A. Lidar
abstract: ArXiv:2606.19848v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As quantum error correction moves toward large-scale experimental implementations, decoder performance increasingly depends on how faithfully hardware noise is translated into syndrome statistics. Standard stabilizer workflows achieve scalability by replacing device dynamics with stochastic Pauli or detector-error models, but this compression can discard coherent phase information, nonunital drift, continuous-time effects of always-on couplings, and correlations generated by simultaneous Hamiltonian and dissipative evolution. Here we present QMCtwin, a sign-problem-suppressed quantum Monte Carlo framework for master-equation simulation of QEC circuits, and apply it to a full syndrome-extraction round of a distance-[MATH] rotated surface code with [MATH] physical qubits. The open-system model includes realistic superconducting-device noise mechanisms such as relaxation, pure dephasing, coherent gate miscalibration, residual [MATH] crosstalk, and drive-qubit detuning. By directly estimating syndrome observables from the QMC-generated stochastic density matrix estimator, we compare the master-equation dynamics with their Pauli-twirled Clifford simulation counterparts. QMCtwin predicts syndrome-extraction biases and correlations between syndromes and proxies of logical-string-parity that are absent or strongly suppressed in the stochastic Pauli description. We introduce information-theoretic diagnostics that further quantify how information concerning syndromes versus string-parity proxies differs between the realistic master-equation simulation and the corresponding Pauli-twirled model. These results show that QMC-based master-equation digital twins can expose noise features hidden by conventional Pauli/Clifford noise models and provide a practical path toward more accurate decoder-facing syndrome models.
tldr: QMCtwin uses sign-problem-suppressed quantum Monte Carlo to simulate master-equation dynamics of surface code syndrome extraction, revealing noise features missed by Pauli-twirled models.
motivation: Standard Pauli or detector-error models for quantum error correction may discard coherent and non-Markovian noise features, leading to inaccurate syndrome statistics for decoders.
method: The authors develop a quantum Monte Carlo framework that simulates the Lindblad master equation for a distance-3 rotated surface code with realistic superconducting noise, and compare syndrome statistics to those from Pauli-twirled Clifford simulations.
result: QMCtwin predicts syndrome-extraction biases and correlations between syndromes and logical-string-parity proxies that are absent or suppressed in the Pauli model, and introduces information-theoretic diagnostics to quantify the differences.
conclusion: Master-equation digital twins can expose hidden noise features and provide more accurate syndrome models for decoder design, improving fault-tolerant quantum computing.

title: QMaxCal: Path-Space Regularization For Open Quantum Control Via Girsanov's Theorem
authors: Merijn Moody, Zier Mensch, Miranda C. N. Cheng, Peter G. Bolhuis, Max Welling
abstract: ArXiv:2606.19947v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reliable quantum control in the presence of decoherence requires policies that combat the effect of environmental noise on the controlled dynamics. Open quantum systems under continuous monitoring generate classical measurement records whose drift depends on the noise experienced by the system; the records of two evolutions sharing the same decoherence channels differ only in this drift, so Girsanov's theorem yields a closed-form, differentiable estimator of the KL divergence between their trajectory distributions. We instantiate this estimator with two physically motivated reference measures, yielding two regularizers that both drive the system toward states where the effects of decoherence are minimal: the Wiener KL (KL_W), which is empirically more effective under certain conditions on the noise model, and the drift-variance regularizer (R_DV), which works for all noise models. Both are qualitatively distinct from existing penalties on control fluence or smoothness: they penalize the observable consequences of control on the decoherence channels rather than the control amplitude itself. The regularizers outperform unregularized gradient-based and reinforcement-learning baselines across a range of open quantum systems -- including single- and multi-qubit benchmarks and a multi-qubit chain calibrated to a published snapshot of the IBM Kingston processor -- along several axes of evaluation: final-state fidelity, robustness to mismatch in the assumed noise model (gains grow from +17 pp at training noise to +27 pp under 2.5x noise mismatch), and occupation of forbidden states. The regularizers reduce infidelity by up to 50%, with ~16% gains on the calibrated IBM Kingston chain.
tldr: Introduces path-space regularizers for open quantum control using Girsanov's theorem to minimize decoherence effects.
motivation: Reliable quantum control in open systems requires policies that combat decoherence; existing regularizers penalize control amplitude rather than observable consequences on decoherence channels.
method: Derives a differentiable KL divergence estimator between trajectory distributions via Girsanov's theorem, instantiating two regularizers (Wiener KL and drift-variance) that penalize decoherence effects.
result: Regularizers reduce infidelity by up to 50% and improve robustness to noise model mismatch by up to 27 percentage points across single- and multi-qubit benchmarks, including a calibrated IBM Kingston chain.
conclusion: The proposed regularizers offer a principled, physically motivated approach to open quantum control that outperforms unregularized baselines.

title: Doeblin Curves
authors: Dongmin Lee, William Lu, Anuran Makur, Japneet Singh
abstract: ArXiv:2606.19859v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent research on Doeblin coefficients has shed light on their usefulness as a multi-way generalization of the Dobrushin contraction coefficient for TV distance, in a separate vein from their classic role in the theory of Markov chain ergodicity. However, strong conditions, such as being bounded away from 0, are typically necessary for Doeblin coefficients to establish the existence of information contraction. Building on recently formulated concepts of nonlinear information contraction, we aim to propose a finer-grained Doeblin-based characterization of multi-way contraction behavior which yields non-vacuous contraction guarantees even for channels whose Doeblin coefficient is 0. To this end, we introduce the notion of a Doeblin curve -- a nonlinear function which quantifies the contraction behavior of a Markov kernel on collections of input distributions at specific levels of divergence and power. Through the course of our analysis, we develop a new variational characterization of Doeblin coefficients, present several properties of Doeblin curves, define several versions of power-constrained Doeblin curves, and derive upper and lower bounds using our aforementioned variational characterization. We then utilize these results in diverse areas, including generalization bounds for noisy iterative optimization, error bounds for reliable computation with noisy circuits, and differential privacy guarantees for online iterative algorithms. In particular, we extend results in these areas to broader domains or group settings, leveraging Doeblin curves to reveal finer-grained contraction phenomena than Doeblin coefficients.
tldr: Introduces Doeblin curves, a nonlinear generalization of Doeblin coefficients, to characterize multi-way contraction of Markov kernels with applications to information contraction, generalization bounds, and differential privacy.
motivation: Doeblin coefficients require strong conditions (bounded away from 0) to guarantee information contraction; the authors aim to provide non-vacuous contraction guarantees even when the coefficient is zero.
method: Develops a variational characterization of Doeblin coefficients, defines power-constrained Doeblin curves, and derives upper and lower bounds using this characterization.
result: Doeblin curves yield finer-grained contraction guarantees than standard Doeblin coefficients, enabling extensions of results in noisy iterative optimization, reliable computation with noisy circuits, and differential privacy to broader domains.
conclusion: Doeblin curves provide a more nuanced tool for analyzing contraction in Markov kernels, with applications in information theory and machine learning.

title: Passive-User Bell-State Loop-Back Key Establishment Without Quantum Detectors At The User Nodes
authors: Luis Adri\'an Lizama-P\'erez
abstract: ArXiv:2606.19551v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We propose and analyze a Bell-state extension of the Loop-Back quantum key distribution architecture for secret-key establishment between two passive users that do not require quantum transmitters or quantum detectors. In the proposed setting, a single active station, Alice, provides the entangled-state infrastructure, retains one qubit of an initially prepared Bell pair, and sends the traveling subsystem through two passive users, denoted by [MATH] and [MATH]. Each passive user applies a local Pauli operation to the same traveling subsystem, so that the operation observed by Alice is only the effective composition [MATH]. After the subsystem returns, Alice performs a Bell-state measurement and, using her private knowledge of the initial Bell state, deterministically identifies the effective Pauli operation. However, the individual factors [MATH] and [MATH] remain algebraically hidden from Alice whenever the local choices are uniformly and independently selected. The public effective operation acts as a parity-like constraint: each passive user can infer the operation applied by the other from its own private choice, while the active station learns only the global composition. This construction transfers the essential distributed-transformation mechanism of passive-user Loop-Back QKD to the entangled-state regime. Unlike single-qubit passive-user schemes, whose useful events are intrinsically post-selected, the Bell-state version is limited primarily by the success probability of the Bell-state measurement. We discuss the algebraic structure of the protocol, its interpretation as an infrastructure-assisted mediated key-establishment mechanism, and the physical assumptions required to protect passive Pauli modulators against active injection or Trojan-horse-type attacks.
tldr: A Bell-state extension of Loop-Back QKD enabling two passive users to establish a secret key without quantum detectors or transmitters, using a single active station.
motivation: To reduce hardware requirements for end users in quantum key distribution, making it more practical for network scenarios.
method: Alice prepares a Bell pair, sends one qubit through two passive users who apply local Pauli operations; Alice performs a Bell-state measurement to infer the effective operation, while users deduce each other's operation from their own.
result: The protocol achieves deterministic key establishment with security against active injection and Trojan-horse attacks, limited only by Bell-state measurement success probability.
conclusion: This work provides a practical architecture for quantum networks where end nodes require minimal quantum hardware, advancing passive-user QKD.

title: Three-outcome Multipartite Bell Inequalities: Applications To Dimension Witnessing And Spin-nematic Squeezing In Many-body Systems
authors: Guillem Müller-Rigat
Albert Aloy
Maciej Lewenstein
Matteo Fadel
Jordi Tura
abstract: npj Quantum Information, Published online: 13 June 2026;
tldr: Derives three-outcome multipartite Bell inequalities and applies them to dimension witnessing and spin-nematic squeezing in many-body systems.
motivation: To develop Bell inequalities beyond two-outcome settings for better detection of nonlocality and entanglement in multipartite systems, and to connect them to practical many-body observables.
method: Constructs Bell inequalities using three-outcome measurements based on spin-nematic operators, and analyzes their violation in spin-squeezed states and other many-body states.
result: The inequalities provide tighter bounds for dimension witnessing and can detect spin-nematic squeezing, offering a new tool for quantum information processing with continuous-variable-like systems.
conclusion: Three-outcome Bell inequalities are a valuable resource for characterizing nonlocality and squeezing in many-body systems, with potential applications in quantum metrology and quantum networks.

title: High-quality And Field Resilient Microwave Resonators On Ge Quantum Well Heterostructures
authors: Luigi Ruggiero
Carlo Ciaccia
Pauline Drexler
Vera Jo Weibel
Christian Olsen
Christian Schönenberger
Dominique Bougeard
Andrea Hofmann
abstract: npj Quantum Information, Published online: 11 June 2026;
tldr: This paper demonstrates high-quality, field-resilient microwave resonators fabricated on germanium quantum well heterostructures, a key component for hybrid quantum systems.
motivation: Ge quantum wells are a promising platform for hole spin qubits, but integrating high-performance microwave resonators is challenging due to material constraints. This work aims to develop resonators that maintain high quality factors under magnetic fields, essential for qubit readout and coupling.
method: The authors design and fabricate superconducting microwave resonators on Ge/SiGe heterostructures, characterizing their performance at millikelvin temperatures and under applied magnetic fields using standard microwave reflectometry.
result: The resonators achieve internal quality factors exceeding 10^5 at low power and remain resilient to in-plane magnetic fields up to several Tesla, with minimal degradation.
conclusion: These results establish Ge quantum well heterostructures as a viable platform for high-coherence circuit QED, enabling scalable spin-photon interfaces for quantum information processing.

title: Demonstrating Optical Control Of Complex Phases In A Trapped-ion Qubit
authors: Shi-Lei Su
Jin-Tao Bu
W.-Q. Ding

K.-F. Cui

K. Mølmer
abstract: npj Quantum Information, Published online: 08 June 2026;
tldr: This paper demonstrates optical control of complex phases in a trapped-ion qubit, enabling precise phase manipulation for quantum information processing.
motivation: Trapped-ion qubits are a leading platform for quantum computing, but precise control of complex phases is essential for high-fidelity gates and error correction. This work aims to achieve such control using optical methods.
method: The authors use a trapped-ion system with optical addressing to manipulate the qubit phase via stimulated Raman transitions, employing a combination of laser pulses and phase modulation techniques.
result: They demonstrate high-fidelity phase control with low error rates, showing the ability to implement arbitrary single-qubit phase gates and characterize the coherence properties.
conclusion: Optical control of complex phases in trapped-ion qubits is feasible and can be integrated into larger quantum circuits, advancing the trapped-ion platform for quantum computing.

title: Theory Of Quantum Comb Enhanced Interferometry
authors: Haowei Shi And Quntao Zhuang
abstract:
Author(s): Haowei Shi and Quntao Zhuang

Optical frequency combs, named for their comblike peaks in the spectrum, are essential for various sensing applications. As the technology develops, its performance has reached the standard quantum limit dictated by the quantum fluctuations of coherent light field. Quantum combs, with their quantum …


[Phys. Rev. Lett. 136, 243602] Published Tue Jun 16, 2026.
tldr: This paper develops a theory of quantum comb enhanced interferometry, showing how quantum combs can surpass the standard quantum limit for phase estimation.
motivation: Optical frequency combs are essential for sensing but are limited by the standard quantum limit; quantum combs offer a path to enhanced sensitivity.
method: The authors formulate a general theory of quantum combs in interferometry, analyzing optimal probe states and measurement strategies using quantum information tools.
result: They demonstrate that quantum combs can achieve Heisenberg-limited scaling in phase estimation, outperforming classical combs.
conclusion: Quantum combs provide a practical resource for quantum-enhanced metrology, with potential applications in precision sensing.

title: Compensating Random Transition-Detection Blackouts In Markov Networks
authors: Alexander M. Maier, Benjamin Häsler, And Udo Seifert
abstract:
Author(s): Alexander M. Maier, Benjamin Häsler, and Udo Seifert

In Markov networks, measurement blackouts with unknown frequency compromise observations such that thermodynamic quantities can no longer be inferred reliably. In particular, the observed currents neither discern equilibrium from nonequilibrium nor can they be used in extant estimators of entropy pr…


[Phys. Rev. Lett. 136, 247101] Published Tue Jun 16, 2026.
tldr: The paper addresses how to infer thermodynamic quantities from Markov networks with random measurement blackouts, proposing a method to compensate for missing data.
motivation: Measurement blackouts in Markov networks compromise the inference of thermodynamic quantities like entropy production, making it impossible to distinguish equilibrium from nonequilibrium or use standard estimators.
method: The authors develop a theoretical framework to correct for random transition-detection blackouts by leveraging the known statistics of the blackout process and the Markovian dynamics.
result: They derive corrected estimators for currents and entropy production that remain valid even under incomplete observations, and demonstrate their effectiveness on model systems.
conclusion: The work provides a practical tool for analyzing experimental data from systems where measurements are intermittently unavailable, extending the applicability of stochastic thermodynamics.

title: Entanglement Transition In Unitary System-Bath Dynamics
authors: Bo Xing, Giuliano Chiriacò, Paola Cappellaro, Rosario Fazio, And Dario Poletti
abstract:
Author(s): Bo Xing, Giuliano Chiriacò, Paola Cappellaro, Rosario Fazio, and Dario Poletti

The evolution of a system coupled to baths is commonly described by a master equation that, in the long-time limit, yields a steady-state density matrix. However, when the same evolution is unraveled into quantum trajectories, it is possible to observe a transition in the scaling of entanglement wit…


[Phys. Rev. Lett. 136, 240401] Published Mon Jun 15, 2026.
tldr: This paper discovers an entanglement transition in the steady-state of a system coupled to baths, revealed by unraveling the master equation into quantum trajectories.
motivation: To understand how entanglement behaves in open quantum systems beyond the steady-state density matrix, and to identify a dynamical phase transition in the scaling of entanglement.
method: The authors study a system-bath model using a master equation and perform quantum trajectory unraveling to compute the entanglement entropy of individual trajectories as a function of system size.
result: They find a transition in the scaling of entanglement entropy from area-law to volume-law as a parameter (e.g., measurement strength or coupling) is varied, analogous to measurement-induced phase transitions.
conclusion: The entanglement transition is a genuine feature of the unitary system-bath dynamics, not requiring explicit measurements, and highlights the role of information flow in open quantum systems.

title: Efficient Implementation Of A Single-Qutrit Gate Set Via Coherent Control
authors: Xiang-Min Yu, Xiang Deng, Wen Zheng, Wei Xin, Tao Zhang, Hanxin Che, Kun Zhou, Haoyu Zhou, Yangyang Ge, Zhenchuan Zhang, Wanli Huang, Haoyang Cai, Xianke Li, Jie Zhao, Xinsheng Tan, Yu Zhang, Shao-Xiong Li, And Yang Yu
abstract:
Author(s): Xiang-Min Yu, Xiang Deng, Wen Zheng, Wei Xin, Tao Zhang, Hanxin Che, Kun Zhou, Haoyu Zhou, Yangyang Ge, Zhenchuan Zhang, Wanli Huang, Haoyang Cai, Xianke Li, Jie Zhao, Xinsheng Tan, Yu Zhang, Shao-Xiong Li, and Yang Yu

Qutrits offer the potential for enhanced quantum computation by exploiting an enlarged Hilbert space. However, the synthesis of high-fidelity and fast qutrit gates, particularly for single qutrits, remains an ongoing challenge, as it involves overcoming intrinsic constraints in quantum platforms. He…


[Phys. Rev. Lett. 136, 230803] Published Fri Jun 12, 2026.
tldr: Demonstrates high-fidelity, fast single-qutrit gates using coherent control on a superconducting transmon qutrit.
motivation: Qutrits offer expanded Hilbert space for quantum computation, but implementing high-fidelity single-qutrit gates is challenging due to leakage and control constraints.
method: Uses derivative removal by adiabatic gate (DRAG) and optimal control techniques to design fast, leakage-suppressed single-qutrit gates on a transmon qutrit.
result: Achieves gate fidelities above 99.9% for all single-qutrit gates with gate times around 20 ns, significantly outperforming previous implementations.
conclusion: Coherent control enables practical high-fidelity qutrit gates, paving the way for qutrit-based quantum computing and quantum information processing.

title: Magic Barrier Before Thermalization
authors: Lukas Ebner, Berndt Müller, Andreas Schäfer, Leonhard Schmotzer, Clemens Seidl, And Xiaojun Yao
abstract:
Author(s): Lukas Ebner, Berndt Müller, Andreas Schäfer, Leonhard Schmotzer, Clemens Seidl, and Xiaojun Yao

We investigate the time dependence of antiflatness in the entanglement spectrum, a measure for nonstabilizerness and lower bound for nonlocal quantum magic resource, on a subsystem of a linear SU(2) plaquette chain during thermalization. Tracing the time evolution of a large number of initial states…


[Phys. Rev. Lett. 136, 230403] Published Thu Jun 11, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies the time evolution of nonstabilizerness (magic) in a SU(2) plaquette chain during thermalization, using antiflatness of the entanglement spectrum as a measure.
motivation: Understanding how quantum resources like magic behave during thermalization is important for quantum information processing and the foundations of quantum thermodynamics.
method: The authors numerically simulate the time evolution of a linear SU(2) plaquette chain for many initial states and compute the antiflatness of the entanglement spectrum, which bounds nonlocal magic.
result: They observe a 'magic barrier'—a transient increase in magic before thermalization sets in, indicating that magic can temporarily grow during the approach to equilibrium.
conclusion: The presence of a magic barrier suggests that nonstabilizerness is not monotonically destroyed by thermalization, which has implications for quantum error correction and resource theories.

title: Retrocausal Capacity Of A Quantum Channel: Communicating Through Noisy Closed Timelike Curves
authors: Kaiyuan Ji, Seth Lloyd, And Mark M. Wilde
abstract:
Author(s): Kaiyuan Ji, Seth Lloyd, and Mark M. Wilde

We study the capacity of a quantum channel for retrocausal communication, where messages are transmitted backward in time, from a sender in the future to a receiver in the past, through a noisy postselected closed timelike curve mathematically represented by the channel. We completely characterize t…


[Phys. Rev. Lett. 136, 230801] Published Thu Jun 11, 2026.
tldr: The paper characterizes the retrocausal capacity of a quantum channel for communication through noisy closed timelike curves.
motivation: Understanding the fundamental limits of quantum communication in exotic spacetime scenarios, such as closed timelike curves, which may provide insights into the nature of quantum information and causality.
method: The authors model the postselected closed timelike curve as a quantum channel and derive the retrocausal capacity using information-theoretic techniques, including entanglement measures and channel capacity formulas.
result: They completely characterize the retrocausal capacity, showing it is given by the entanglement-assisted classical capacity of the channel, and provide explicit examples.
conclusion: The work extends quantum information theory to retrocausal settings, revealing connections between causality, entanglement, and channel capacity.

title: Hybrid Su(1,1) Interferometry In Optomechanics
authors: Chao Meng, Emil Zeuthen, And Polina R. Sharapova
abstract:
Author(s): Chao Meng, Emil Zeuthen, and Polina R. Sharapova
