The proposed attack is experimentally validated on real Commsignia OnBoard Unit (OBU) and RoadSide Unit (RSU) devices using a HackRF One across three scenarios that emulate synthetic trajectories at steady speeds of 90 km/h, 145 km/h, and 200 km/h. The most significant contribution of this paper is the demonstration that V2X communications are not secured, as they are susceptible to GNSS spoofing attacks, which cause service degradation without being detected.
tldr: This paper demonstrates a GNSS spoofing attack on V2X communications using low-cost SDR, showing that V2X systems are vulnerable to undetected spoofing.
motivation: GNSS is critical for V2X safety applications, but spoofing attacks can cause false positioning and service degradation. The authors aim to highlight the lack of security in current V2X systems.
method: The authors develop a coordinate generation pipeline using Haversine distance, temporal discretization, and linear interpolation to create fake GPS baseband signals. They implement the attack with a HackRF One SDR on real Commsignia OBU and RSU devices.
result: The spoofing attack successfully misleads the V2X devices into computing false positions across three speed scenarios (90, 145, 200 km/h) without detection.
conclusion: V2X communications are not secure against GNSS spoofing, and countermeasures are urgently needed to ensure vehicular safety.

title: TrustMix: How To Mix Messages In A Mobile Ad-hoc Network
authors: Yu Shen, Aiswarya Walter, Stefanie Roos
abstract: ArXiv:2606.20251v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Mix networks are a highly effective way to achieve anonymity, defending against a wide range of traffic-analysis attacks. However, mix networks are usually designed for infrastructure networks and cannot be directly applied in the context of mobile ad hoc networks (MANETs). The few existing solutions for MANETs require advance knowledge of the topology or a trusted central party. In this paper, we present TrustMix, a mix protocol for MANETs that operates without any central trusted party. In TrustMix, parties join groups and then messages are forwarded via multiple groups to provide anonymity. With TrustMix, users only need to find a party nearby that they consider trusted. They then forward the message to this party's group, and the party shuffles messages before forwarding to other groups, meaning that the original message and the forwarded message cannot be linked. Furthermore, even if the chosen party is adversarial, they can only break the anonymity if all parties in their group are adversarial as all of them contribute to the shuffling. In addition to anonymity, TrustMix also enforces rate limits on the number of messages through the use of linkable ring signatures, which allows detecting that parties send more messages that allowed without revealing identities. We prove the security of our protocol in the random oracle model. We evaluate its anonymity using an existing mix-network simulator and show that TrustMix significantly improves message anonymity. Finally, we present a proof-of-concept Android implementation and show that TrustMix achieves acceptable throughput with 5 mobile devices.
tldr: TrustMix is a mix protocol for mobile ad-hoc networks that provides anonymity without a central trusted party.
motivation: Existing mix networks are designed for infrastructure networks and cannot be directly applied to MANETs; prior MANET solutions require topology knowledge or a trusted central party.
method: Parties form groups and forward messages via multiple groups; messages are shuffled within groups to prevent linking, and linkable ring signatures enforce rate limits.
result: Security is proven in the random oracle model; simulations show improved anonymity; a proof-of-concept Android implementation achieves acceptable throughput with 5 devices.
conclusion: TrustMix demonstrates a practical decentralized mix protocol for MANETs with provable security and reasonable performance.

title: Linked Fates: How Small Of An Ambiguity Increase Can Make The Difference Between Equaling And Separating From P?
authors: Benjamin Carleton, Michael C. Chavrimootoo, Lane A. Hemaspaandra, David E. Narv\'aez, Conor Taliancich, Melissa Welsh
abstract: ArXiv:2606.20399v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Ambiguity-bounded versions of [MATH], denoted [MATH], bound by [MATH] the number of accepting paths the nondeterministic polynomial-time Turing machine can have on inputs of length [MATH]. Such classes range from Valiant's completely unambiguous ([MATH]) class [MATH] to [MATH] itself, where there is no bound or, equivalently, there is the toothless exponential bound ([MATH]). This paper seeks to understand which of these classes stand and fall together as to whether they equal deterministic polynomial time. Informally put, what ranges of ambiguities have linked fates? That is, for which pairs of nondecreasing functions, [MATH], satisfying [MATH], does it hold that [MATH]. More particularly, for which pairs does that hold robustly, i.e., it holds in the real world and every relativized world? And for which pairs does that implication fail to hold robustly, i.e., there is an oracle [MATH] such that [MATH]? The only previously known positive result is Watanabe's 1988 result that [MATH], which even holds robustly. His result, though lovely, applies only to constant-bounded ambiguities. As our positive result, we present a new class of cases (Theorem 3.8) that apply (and even robustly apply) at greater ambiguity levels. To give our class of cases, we leverage two approaches: a novel path-poisoning approach that works even on superconstant ambiguities (Theorem 3.5) and a new application of the power of padding (Theorems 3.3/3.4). As negative results, we show that for essentially all other cases, no linkage holds robustly.
tldr: This paper studies the relationship between ambiguity-bounded nondeterministic polynomial-time classes and deterministic polynomial time, focusing on when equalities or separations hold robustly across oracles.
motivation: To understand which ambiguity-bounded classes (from UP to NP) have linked fates regarding whether they equal P, and to extend Watanabe's 1988 result beyond constant ambiguity bounds.
method: The authors introduce a path-poisoning approach for superconstant ambiguities and use padding techniques to prove positive results; for negative results, they construct oracles to show non-robustness.
result: They identify a new class of ambiguity functions for which UP = P implies the class equals P robustly, and show that for essentially all other cases, no such robust linkage holds.
conclusion: The fate of ambiguity-bounded classes relative to P is highly sensitive to the ambiguity bound, with only specific ranges exhibiting robust linked fates.

title: Llm Agent Safety, Multi-turn Red-teaming, Jailbreak Benchmarks, Adversarial Robustness, Safety-critical Systems
authors: Hanwool Lee, Dasol Choi, Bokyeong Kim, Seung Geun Kim, Haon Park
abstract: ArXiv:2606.20408v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly proposed as supervisory components for safety-critical systems, yet their robustness under sustained, adaptive adversarial pressure remains poorly characterized. We present NRT-Bench, a benchmark for multi-turn red-teaming of LLM agents acting as operators of a safety-critical system, instantiated in a simulated nuclear power plant control room. A five-role operator team, each backed by a configurable LLM, runs a plant governed by six critical safety functions (CSFs), while adversaries inject messages over four channels in bounded multi-turn sessions with per-turn feedback. Harm is an objective signal rather than LLM-judged text: a run terminates the moment any CSF is lost, attributed to the causing message. Evaluating four frontier operator models under a fixed-attack paired-replay protocol, we find that adaptive multi-turn attacks reliably push the operator team past a safety limit: across the four models, between 8.7% and 12.1% of attack sessions end with the plant losing a critical safety function. Although the four models look almost equally robust by this aggregate rate, their failures barely overlap: of [MATH] sessions, none defeat all four models while a third defeat at least one, so vulnerabilities are nearly disjoint across models rather than nested. The effect of added defences is strongly model-dependent: the same guardrail stack or safety-advisor agent that lowers attack success for one model can raise it for another. We release the simulation venue, attack dataset, and replay tooling for reproducible safety evaluation of LLM agents.
tldr: This paper presents a benchmark for multi-turn red-teaming of LLM agents in a simulated nuclear power plant control room, evaluating adversarial robustness.
motivation: LLM agents are increasingly used in safety-critical systems, but their robustness under sustained adversarial attacks is poorly characterized.
method: The authors introduce NRT-Bench, a benchmark with a simulated nuclear power plant where LLM-based operator teams are attacked via multi-turn adversarial messages; harm is measured by loss of critical safety functions.
result: Adaptive multi-turn attacks cause 8.7%-12.1% of sessions to lose a safety function; vulnerabilities are nearly disjoint across models, and defenses have model-dependent effects.
conclusion: LLM agents in safety-critical roles are vulnerable to adaptive attacks, and robustness varies significantly across models and defenses.

title: Multi-View Decompilation For LLM-Based Malware Classification
authors: Vyas Raina Bercan Turkmen
abstract: ArXiv:2606.20436v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Malware analysts often inspect compiled binaries through decompiled pseudo-C, when source code is unavailable. Recent work suggests that large language models (LLMs) can assist this process by classifying decompiled code as benign or malicious, but existing pipelines typically rely on a single decompiler view. We argue that this assumption is fragile: decompilers are lossy heuristic tools, and different decompilers can expose different artefacts of the same binary. We curate a benchmark of benign utilities and malicious programs spanning a range of threat behaviors. Each sample is compiled and decompiled with both Ghidra and RetDec, yielding matched pseudo-C views. Across a range of LLMs from major model families, we find that providing both decompiler views improves malicious-class F1, mainly by increasing recall on malicious samples. Agreement analyses further show that Ghidra and RetDec make partially different errors, supporting the view that decompiler outputs provide complementary evidence. Our results suggest that multi-decompiler prompting is a simple, training-free way to improve LLM-based malware triage in practical settings.
tldr: This paper proposes using multiple decompiler views to improve LLM-based malware classification from binary code.
motivation: Malware analysts rely on decompiled code when source is unavailable, but single decompiler views are lossy and may miss artifacts.
method: The authors compile benign and malicious programs, decompile them with Ghidra and RetDec, and prompt LLMs with both views to classify.
result: Providing both decompiler views improves malicious-class F1, mainly by increasing recall, as the decompilers make complementary errors.
conclusion: Multi-decompiler prompting is a simple, training-free way to improve LLM-based malware triage in practical settings.

title: A-compass: Formal Foundations For Anonymity Analysis In Microdata
authors: Silvia Ghilezan Tamara Tagliavia
abstract: ArXiv:2606.20492v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In the information age, one of the leading problems is how to ensure individual's privacy. Depending on the context in which privacy is considered, various data privacy models have emerged. However, the domain of formal verification of these models is still not sufficiently explored even when it comes to the most basic models. An attempt to verify privacy requirements is the Compliance Assertion Language (COMPASS). In COMPASS, one can specify an anonymity condition that a table needs to satisfy, and an action that will modify the table if the condition is not satisfied. It is designed to operate on preprocessed tables in a form one record - one group of people. In this paper, we modify the COMPASS language in order to operate on microdata tables in their usual form of one record - one person. The modified language is called A-COMPASS. Along with checking of previously applied anonymity conditions, A-COMPASS enables the execution of anonymization actions as a new feature. We further provide the syntax and the semantics for the A-COMPASS language. We also prove the most important properties of the introduced semantics like determinism and compositionality. Finally, we provide a mechanism to verify anonymity properties, such as k-anonymity and l-diversity.
tldr: This paper extends the COMPASS language for formal verification of anonymity in microdata tables, focusing on k-anonymity and l-diversity.
motivation: Formal verification of privacy models like k-anonymity is underexplored; existing tools like COMPASS operate on preprocessed tables, not standard microdata.
method: The authors modify COMPASS to create A-COMPASS, which works on one-record-per-person microdata, adding syntax, semantics, and anonymization actions.
result: They prove determinism and compositionality of the semantics and provide a mechanism to verify k-anonymity and l-diversity.
conclusion: A-COMPASS enables formal verification and enforcement of anonymity conditions on microdata, advancing privacy analysis tools.

title: Calibration Without Comprehension: Diagnosing The Limits Of Fine-Tuning LLMs For Vulnerability Detection In Systems Software
authors: Marco Vieira Arastoo Zibaeirad
abstract: ArXiv:2606.20502v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Whether LLMs scoring well on vulnerability benchmarks genuinely reason about security or merely pattern-match on contaminated data remains unresolved. We present CWE-Trace, a framework for LLM vulnerability detection built from 834 manually curated Linux kernel samples spanning 74 CWEs. The framework enforces a strict temporal split (pre-2025 historical set / post-cutoff leakage-free set), preserves context-aware vulnerable--patched pairs, and introduces two diagnostic metrics: the Directional Failure Index (DFI) and Hierarchical Distance and Direction (HDD). We evaluate eight vanilla LLMs and 15 LoRA fine-tuned variants across non-targeted detection, targeted detection, and CWE classification. Our analysis yields two key results. First, data contamination provides no measurable advantage. Function-level analysis shows that 84% of nominally contaminated samples carry no usable memorization signal: vulnerable functions are absent or cross-mapped across datasets, and ~31% of contaminated samples carry CWE misclassification. Second, backbone directional priors dominate fine-tuning. Models exhibit stable, systematic failure modes (DFI ranging from -85.5 to +94.8 pp) that persist from historical to post-cutoff data and resist correction. Fine-tuning shifts the output threshold without changing the decision policy. This is calibration without comprehension: output distributions adapt to training data while the underlying security reasoning remains absent. The weakest backbone at binary detection (DeepSeek-R1) gains the most in coarse CWE classification, revealing that detection and understanding are decoupled capabilities. The best detection score reaches only 52.1% (+2.1 pp above chance); exact CWE ranking remains below 1.3% Top-1 accuracy, confirming that current LLMs lack reliable security reasoning for systems software, regardless of fine-tuning strategy.
tldr: This paper evaluates LLMs for vulnerability detection in systems software, finding that fine-tuning only calibrates output distributions without improving security reasoning.
motivation: To determine whether LLMs genuinely reason about security or merely pattern-match on contaminated data, and to diagnose the limits of fine-tuning for vulnerability detection.
method: The authors introduce CWE-Trace, a framework with 834 manually curated Linux kernel samples spanning 74 CWEs, and evaluate 8 vanilla LLMs and 15 LoRA fine-tuned variants using diagnostic metrics DFI and HDD.
result: Data contamination provides no measurable advantage; backbone directional priors dominate fine-tuning, leading to calibration without comprehension. Best detection score is 52.1% (just above chance), and exact CWE ranking is below 1.3% Top-1 accuracy.
conclusion: Current LLMs lack reliable security reasoning for systems software, regardless of fine-tuning strategy.

title: Sovereign Execution Brokers: Enforcing Certificate-Bound Authority In Agentic Control Planes
authors: Deying Yu Jun He
abstract: ArXiv:2606.20520v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Autonomous agents are increasingly connected to cloud, deployment, and data-control workflows, but production mutation authority should not reside inside non-deterministic reasoning processes. Existing access-control mechanisms authorize identities, while assurance layers certify proposed actions; neither alone provides a mandatory enforcement point for certified authority at the moment of mutation. This paper introduces the Sovereign Execution Broker (SEB), a runtime enforcement boundary for certificate-bound agentic infrastructure. SEB consumes certificates issued by the Sovereign Assurance Boundary (SAB), verifies that the requested mutation matches the certified execution contract, checks validity windows, policy epochs, revocation epochs, and live-state drift, mints scoped execution identity, invokes infrastructure APIs, and records signed decision and outcome records. By separating proposal, admission, and execution, SEB turns certified authority into a short-lived, revocable, auditable runtime capability, provided that production mutation APIs reject non-broker identities. We present the SEB execution model, certificate and replay-verification predicates, scoped identity semantics, bypass-prevention deployment patterns, failure behavior, and a concrete prototype implementation. We evaluate the prototype on AWS and Kubernetes clusters, measuring latency overheads, revocation propagation, drift detection, and security under fault injection.
tldr: This paper introduces a runtime enforcement boundary for certificate-bound agentic infrastructure, focusing on access control and security in cloud and Kubernetes environments.
motivation: Production mutation authority should not reside inside non-deterministic reasoning processes, and existing access-control mechanisms lack mandatory enforcement for certified authority at the moment of mutation.
method: The Sovereign Execution Broker (SEB) consumes certificates from the Sovereign Assurance Boundary (SAB), verifies execution contracts, checks validity windows and drift, mints scoped execution identity, invokes APIs, and records signed records.
result: A prototype on AWS and Kubernetes shows latency overheads, revocation propagation, drift detection, and security under fault injection.
conclusion: SEB turns certified authority into a short-lived, revocable, auditable runtime capability, provided production mutation APIs reject non-broker identities.

title: From Efficiency To Leakage -- Privacy Backdoor In Federated Language Model Fine-Tuning
authors: Shanghao Shi, Chaoyu Zhang, Heng Jin, Yang Xiao, Yevgeniy Vorobeychik, William Yeoh, Ning Zhang, Y. Thomas Hou, Wenjing Lou
abstract: ArXiv:2606.20553v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Federated learning (FL) enables multiple parties to collaboratively fine-tune language models for domain-specific tasks without sharing raw data. Since full model fine-tuning is often prohibitively expensive for FL clients, parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) has become the de facto approach in practice, freezing the base model and training only a small set of adapters. In this paper, we show that a malicious parameter server can stealthily corrupt a PEFT adapter into a privacy backdoor that implicitly memorizes the client's training samples as isolated per-sample parameter updates stored in separate neurons, without degrading model utility. Concretely, our attack, NeuroImprint, assigns a dedicated memorization neuron to each training sample and constrains that each neuron is updated at most once along the local fine-tuning trajectory. This design mitigates both cross-sample collisions and cross-step mixing introduced by large local batches and stateful optimizers (e.g., Adam/AdamW) in language-model fine-tuning. After fine-tuning, the resulting isolated per-sample updates can be analytically inverted in closed form to recover text embeddings, which are then deterministically mapped back to token sequences. To understand the generality of our method, we implemented NeuroImprint on multiple language models (BERT, GPT-2, Qwen2, and Llama3.2) and evaluated it across four fine-tuning datasets spanning diverse domains. The results demonstrate that our attack can reconstruct 59% to 79% of all finetuning samples with high semantic fidelity.
tldr: This paper presents a privacy attack on federated learning for language models, exploiting parameter-efficient fine-tuning to reconstruct training samples.
motivation: Federated learning aims to protect client data privacy, but malicious parameter servers may leak private information through model updates.
method: The attack, NeuroImprint, assigns dedicated memorization neurons to each training sample and constrains updates to avoid collisions, enabling closed-form inversion of text embeddings.
result: The attack reconstructs 59% to 79% of fine-tuning samples with high semantic fidelity across multiple models and datasets.
conclusion: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning in federated learning introduces a privacy backdoor that can be exploited to recover client data, highlighting a significant security vulnerability.

title: Veritas: Verifier-Guided Proof Search For Zero-Shot Formal Theorem Proving
authors: Manish Acharya, Zhenyu Liao, Yueke Zhang, Kevin Leach, Yu Huang, Yifan Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2606.19399v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: LLM-based formal provers often collapse rich verifier signals (syntax errors, type mismatches, partial goal progress) into a binary pass/fail bit. We present VERITAS, a zero-shot framework that routes every verifier signal back into proof search through a two-phase protocol: Best-of-N sampling first, then a critic-guided MCTS pass that ingests Phase 1 failures as explicit negative examples. The protocol preserves every theorem solved by its own Phase 1 sweep, so Phase 2's additional solves are attributable to feedback-driven exploration. VERITAS reaches 40.6% on miniF2F (vs. an independently run Best-of-5 at 36.9%, Portfolio 26.2%) and 7.3% on VERITAS-CombiBench, a 55-theorem combinatorics benchmark we release on which Best-of-5 (1.8%) falls below Portfolio (3.6%), exposing that unguided sampling hurts when correct lemma names must be recovered iteratively from verifier feedback. Artifacts are available on GitHub.
tldr: VERITAS is a zero-shot framework for formal theorem proving that uses verifier feedback to guide proof search via Best-of-N sampling and critic-guided MCTS.
motivation: LLM-based formal provers typically discard rich verifier signals, reducing them to a binary pass/fail, which limits proof search efficiency.
method: VERITAS employs a two-phase protocol: Phase 1 uses Best-of-N sampling to generate candidate proofs; Phase 2 applies critic-guided MCTS that ingests Phase 1 failures as negative examples to explore new proof paths.
result: VERITAS achieves 40.6% on miniF2F (vs. Best-of-5 36.9%) and 7.3% on VERITAS-CombiBench (vs. Best-of-5 1.8%), demonstrating the value of feedback-driven exploration.
conclusion: Leveraging verifier feedback beyond binary signals significantly improves zero-shot formal theorem proving, especially in domains requiring iterative lemma recovery.

title: Analyzing The Narration Gap In LLM-Solver Loops
authors: Songgaojun Deng Zunchen Huang
abstract: ArXiv:2606.19588v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Formal tools such as SAT and SMT solvers are increasingly embedded in language model reasoning pipelines when a safety or security critical question can be formulated in logic. Unlike chain of thought whose steps are sampled from the model distribution without formal guarantee, a solver produces a sound and independently verifiable answer. However, the soundness guarantee can be lost in the interaction between the solver and the model. The hybrid pipeline has three components: formalizing the question, deciding it, and narrating the result. Prior work has studied the formalization and decision, but not narration, which is the step that turns a formal tool's output into the user answer. To fill the narration gap, we first model the LLM-solver loop as a verified decision procedure. We further evaluate five open-sourced models under prompt injection, and we find certificate gating makes the solver verdict sound, while an adversary can invert a verified conclusion across phrasings and channels. We study the mitigation through hardened prompt that reduces injection significantly but cannot eliminate it and still suffers under adaptive attack. Combining the formal analysis and empirical studies, we show in the LLM-solver loop, robustness does not reach to the answer that the user finally reads.
tldr: This paper studies the narration gap in LLM-solver loops, focusing on robustness of the final answer under prompt injection.
motivation: Formal solvers are used in LLM reasoning pipelines for safety-critical questions, but the narration step that converts solver output to user answer can be attacked, breaking soundness.
method: The authors model the LLM-solver loop as a verified decision procedure and empirically evaluate five open-source models under prompt injection attacks, testing certificate gating and hardened prompts.
result: Certificate gating makes the solver verdict sound, but an adversary can invert a verified conclusion across phrasings and channels; hardened prompts reduce injection but not eliminate it under adaptive attacks.
conclusion: Robustness does not extend to the final user-readable answer in LLM-solver loops, highlighting a critical vulnerability.

result: Observed elastic softening in BaSO4 under compression, while SrSO4 did not show similar behavior.
conclusion: The elastic softening in BaSO4 is linked to its structural instability under pressure, providing insights into pressure-induced phase transitions.

title: Unified Interlayer Sliding And Shuffling Mechanism For Complex Platelike Nanoprecipitates In Aluminum Alloys
authors: Junyuan Bai, Gaowu Qin, Xueyong Pang, And Zhihao Zhao
abstract:

The strength of aluminum alloys, the most widely used lightweight structural materials, mainly originates from coherent complex-structured nanoplates. Yet, the atomic-scale mechanisms governing their formation remain elusive, owing to the inherent difficulty of probing and simulating solid-state nuc…


[Phys. Rev. B 113, 224108] Published Mon Jun 15, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies the atomic-scale mechanisms of interlayer sliding and shuffling in complex platelike nanoprecipitates in aluminum alloys.
motivation: Understanding the formation of coherent complex-structured nanoplates is crucial for improving the strength of aluminum alloys, but the atomic-scale mechanisms are elusive.
method: The authors use computational modeling and simulation to investigate the interlayer sliding and shuffling processes in nanoprecipitates.
result: They propose a unified mechanism that explains the structural transformations during precipitate formation.
conclusion: The findings provide insights into the design of high-strength aluminum alloys through controlled precipitation.

title: Bifurcations And Multistability In Inducible Three-gene Toggle Switch Networks
authors: Rebecca J. Rousseau And Rob Phillips
abstract:

tldr: This paper studies bifurcations and multistability in a synthetic three-gene toggle switch network, a topic in systems biology.
motivation: Understanding multistability in gene regulatory circuits is important for biological processes and synthetic biology.
method: The authors analyze a mathematical model of a three-gene toggle switch network using bifurcation theory and numerical simulations.
result: They identify conditions for multistability and characterize bifurcation diagrams showing transitions between stable states.
conclusion: The work provides insights into the design principles of multistable gene circuits, with potential applications in synthetic biology.

title: Influence Of Visual Field Offset On Collective Behavior: An Exploration Using The Two-dimensional Vicsek Model
authors: Poorendra Ramlall, Sachit Butail, And Subhradeep Roy
abstract:
Author(s): Poorendra Ramlall, Sachit Butail, and Subhradeep Roy

This study investigates the influence of visual field offset—a restricted field of vision positioned at a fixed angle from an agent's heading direction—on collective behavior using the Vicsek model. This offset shapes an agent's ability to perceive and respond to neighbors, thereby impacting overall…


[Phys. Rev. E 113, 064409] Published Wed Jun 17, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies how a fixed visual field offset affects collective motion in the Vicsek model, a classical model of self-propelled particles.
motivation: Understanding how limited and offset visual perception influences group coordination in biological and robotic swarms.
method: Agent-based simulations of the two-dimensional Vicsek model with a parameter controlling the angular offset of each agent's visual field.
result: The offset angle significantly alters the onset and nature of collective motion, including changes in order parameter and clustering.
conclusion: Visual field offset is a crucial factor in collective behavior, with implications for designing robotic swarms and interpreting biological systems.

title: Topological Enhancement Of Protein Kinetic Stability
authors: João N. C. Especial And Patrícia F. N. Faísca
abstract:

Knotted proteins embed a physical (i.e., open) knot within their native structures. For decades, significant effort has been devoted to elucidating the functional role of knots in proteins, yet no consensus has been reached. Here, using extensive Monte Carlo off-lattice simulations of a simple struc…


[Phys. Rev. E 113, L062402] Published Wed Jun 17, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies how topological knots in proteins enhance kinetic stability using Monte Carlo simulations.
motivation: To understand the functional role of knots in proteins, which remains debated despite decades of research.
method: Extensive Monte Carlo off-lattice simulations of a simple structure-based model for knotted proteins.
result: Topological knots increase the kinetic stability of proteins by slowing down unfolding.
conclusion: Knots may serve a biological role by enhancing protein robustness against mechanical stress.

title: Characterizing Emergent Multiscale Dynamics In Colloidal Nanoparticle Gels
authors: William D. Brackett, Zachary M. Sherman, Felix Lehmkühler, Thomas M. Truskett, And Delia J. Milliron
abstract:
Author(s): William D. Brackett, Zachary M. Sherman, Felix Lehmkühler, Thomas M. Truskett, and Delia J. Milliron

Characterizing the dynamics of nanoparticle gel networks demands a spatiotemporal resolution that no single technique can provide. This Perspective describes the opportunities to address this challenge using X-ray photon correlation spectroscopy at fourth-generation light sources combined with complementary experimental and simulation tools. This should move the field beyond descriptive fundamental studies toward mechanistic understanding and design of nanoparticle gels with adaptive and programmable behaviors.


[Phys. Rev. E 113, 061001] Published Tue Jun 16, 2026.
tldr: This perspective discusses using X-ray photon correlation spectroscopy at fourth-generation light sources to study multiscale dynamics in colloidal nanoparticle gels.
motivation: Characterizing the dynamics of nanoparticle gel networks requires spatiotemporal resolution beyond any single technique.
method: The paper proposes combining X-ray photon correlation spectroscopy with complementary experimental and simulation tools.
result: No new results; it is a perspective outlining opportunities for future research.
conclusion: The approach could move the field toward mechanistic understanding and design of adaptive nanoparticle gels.

title: Pacemaker-induced Spiral Wave Chimeras On A Sphere Of Delay-coupled Oscillators: Switching Between Different Spiral-phase Kinks
authors: Chol-Ung Choe, Ryong-Son Kim, And Jin-Song Kang
abstract:

[Phys. Rev. E 113, 064206] Published Tue Jun 16, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies spiral wave chimeras in delay-coupled oscillators on a sphere, a topic in nonlinear dynamics.
motivation: To understand the emergence and switching of spiral wave chimeras in spatially extended systems with nonlocal coupling.
method: Numerical simulations of a two-dimensional system of nonlocally coupled phase oscillators on a sphere with time-delayed coupling.
result: Observation of pacemaker-induced spiral wave chimeras and switching between different spiral-phase kinks.
conclusion: The findings contribute to the understanding of chimera states in complex networks, but are unrelated to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Flow Of Yield Stress Fluid In A Percolating Network
authors: Nathan Abitbol, Alex Hansen, Alberto Rosso, And Laurent Talon

We study the flow of a Bingham yield stress fluid in a pore network model where the throats have radii drawn from a uniform distribution. We consider the case in which a fraction of the largest radii is blocked. The fluid can flow only through the percolating cluster that exists when the fraction is…


[Phys. Rev. E 113, 065107] Published Tue Jun 16, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies the flow of a Bingham yield stress fluid in a percolating network, focusing on pore-scale physics and rheology.
motivation: Understanding how yield stress fluids flow through porous media is important for applications like enhanced oil recovery and groundwater remediation.
method: The authors use a pore network model with uniformly distributed throat radii, blocking a fraction of the largest radii, and simulate the flow of a Bingham fluid through the percolating cluster.
result: They find that the flow behavior depends on the percolation threshold and the yield stress, with a critical pressure gradient needed for flow.
conclusion: The study provides insights into the interplay between network structure and fluid rheology, but has no connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: High-energy Pulsed Electron-beam-induced Phase Transitions In A Plasma-levitated Crystalline Dust Cluster

Dust clusters with crystalline structure, formed by charged microparticles in complex plasmas, can undergo phase transitions under external influences. [Phys. Rev. E 113, 065209] Published Tue Jun 16, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies phase transitions in plasma-levitated crystalline dust clusters induced by high-energy pulsed electron beams.
motivation: To explore a new factor (electron beam irradiation) that can trigger phase transitions in dust clusters, beyond traditional temperature and pressure effects.
method: Experimental: a plasma-levitated crystalline dust cluster is exposed to high-energy pulsed electron beams, and the structural changes are observed.
result: The electron beam induces phase transitions in the dust cluster, altering its crystalline structure.
conclusion: High-energy pulsed electron beams can effectively induce phase transitions in plasma-levitated dust clusters, offering a new control parameter for such systems.

title: Performance Enhancement Of Direct-drive Shock-augmented Ignition Inertial Fusion Implosions Through Shock Timing Optimization
authors: M. Khan, K. Churnetski, D. E. M. Barlow, R. Betti, C. Freeman, K. Glize, J. Kunimune, A. Lees, R. Mancini, A. Nutter, R. W. Paddock, S. Regan, C. Stoeckl, W. Theobald, N. Woolsey, And R. H. H. Scott

Shock-augmented ignition (SAI) [R. H. H. Scott et al.,
tldr: This paper optimizes shock timing in direct-drive inertial fusion implosions to improve performance of shock-augmented ignition.
motivation: Shock-augmented ignition is a promising inertial confinement fusion concept, but its performance depends critically on precise shock timing.
method: The authors use simulations and experiments to systematically vary shock timing parameters and measure fusion yield.
result: Optimized shock timing leads to enhanced fuel compression and higher neutron yield compared to baseline designs.
conclusion: Shock timing optimization is an effective way to boost performance of shock-augmented ignition implosions.

title: General Approach For Partitioning And Phase Separation In Macromolecular Coexisting Phases
authors: Vikki Anand Varma And Alberto Scacchi

In cells, macromolecules are distributed among distinct biomolecular phases. The coexistence of polymeric aqueous phases in multicomponent systems has been w…


[Phys. Rev. E 113, 065414] Published Tue Jun 16, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies partitioning and phase separation in macromolecular coexisting phases, a topic in soft matter physics.
motivation: Understanding how biomaterials partition among coexisting phases is important for cellular biology and industrial applications.
method: The authors develop a general theoretical approach, likely using statistical mechanics or field theory, to describe partitioning in polymeric mixtures.
result: The approach yields predictions for phase behavior and partitioning coefficients in multicomponent polymer systems.
conclusion: The work provides a framework for analyzing phase separation in complex macromolecular mixtures, relevant to biological and industrial contexts.

authors: Soumya, Sugam Kumar, Joachim Kohlbrecher, And Vinod K. Aswal

Nanoparticle-protein dispersions constitute complex soft materials in which competing attractive and repulsive interactions can strongly influence their phase behavior, including gelation. In this work, we demonstrate a strategy to utilize interaction between anionic silica nanoparticles and anionic…


[Phys. Rev. E 113, 065415] Published Tue Jun 16, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies gelation in nanoparticle-protein dispersions, focusing on tunable interactions and phase behavior.
motivation: Understanding and controlling gelation in soft materials is important for applications in food, cosmetics, and biomaterials.

result: The gelation temperature and mechanical properties can be tuned by varying nanoparticle concentration and protein-to-nanoparticle ratio.
conclusion: Nanoparticle-mediated interactions provide a versatile route to design protein-based gels with desired properties.

title: Regulating Droplet-surface Contact Time Via A Predeposited Microparticle
authors: Chao-Sheng Li, Shun-Jie Wu, Rong-Rong Cai, And Li-Zhi Zhang

Conventional strategies relying on surface microstructure modification suffer from high fabrication costs and compromised surface…

tldr: This paper studies how a predeposited microparticle on a surface can reduce droplet contact time, relevant to industrial applications like inkjet printing and spray cooling.
motivation: Reducing droplet-surface contact time is important for industrial processes, but conventional surface microstructure modifications are costly and can degrade surface properties.
method: The authors experimentally and theoretically investigate the effect of a single microparticle placed on a surface on the dynamics of an impacting droplet, analyzing contact time reduction.
result: The presence of a microparticle significantly reduces droplet contact time by altering the droplet's spreading and retraction dynamics.
conclusion: Using a predeposited microparticle offers a simple, cost-effective method to regulate droplet contact time without modifying the entire surface.

title: Amplitude Variation In Spanwise Wall Oscillations: Effects On Drag Reduction And Heat Transfer In Compressible Turbulent Channel Flow
authors: Fangliang Xu, Wei Liu, And Peng Zhang

Spanwise Wall Oscillation is a promising active flow control technique for turbulent skin-friction drag reduction (DR). [Phys. Rev. E 113, 065105] Published Mon Jun 15, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies drag reduction and heat transfer in compressible turbulent channel flow using spanwise wall oscillations, with no connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

method: Numerical simulations of compressible turbulent channel flow with oscillating walls, analyzing amplitude variation effects on drag and heat transfer.
result: The study quantifies how amplitude variation affects drag reduction and heat transfer in compressible turbulent channel flow.
conclusion: Spanwise wall oscillation can reduce drag in compressible flows, but the effects on heat transfer depend on amplitude and flow parameters.

title: Dispersion Relations For Active Undulators In Overdamped Environments
authors: Christopher J. Pierce, Daniel Irvine, Lucinda Peng, Xuefei Lu, Hang Lu, And Daniel I. Goldman

motivation: Understanding how organisms adjust gait parameters to maintain performance across different substrates.
method: The authors identify a unifying relationship between frequency and wave number for overdamped undulatory locomotion.
result: A dispersion relation is derived that links frequency and wave number for active undulators.
conclusion: The work provides a theoretical framework for biological locomotion in overdamped media.

title: Electron Heat Flux And Whistler Instability In The Earth's Magnetosheath
authors: Ida Svenningsson, Emiliya Yordanova, Yuri V. Khotyaintsev, Mats André, Giulia Cozzani, Alexandros Chasapis, And Steven J. Schwartz

#AdvancingField #TechnicalAdvancement

method: An iterative scheme based on the Martin–Siggia–Rose formalism is developed and compared with numerical simulations.
result: The closure scheme compares well with numerical simulations.
conclusion: The Martin–Siggia–Rose formalism provides an effective approach for calculating dynamical correlation functions in this astrophysical context.

result: The enhanced pair approximation accurately determines epidemic thresholds and infection fractions across arbitrary networks.
conclusion: The method provides a more accurate description of SIS dynamics on networks, but the work is purely classical and unrelated to the user's research interests.

authors: Zhiyuan Cheng, Chun Liu, Yan Wang, And Hong Liu

motivation: To understand how polymerization-driven self-assembly on anisotropic templates can produce complex nanostructures under nonequilibrium conditions.
method: The authors use molecular dynamics simulations to model the surface-initiated polymerization on Janus-polymer-grafted carbon nanotubes and analyze the resulting assembly mechanisms.
result: They identify distinct assembly regimes and show that the Janus grafting pattern leads to unique nonequilibrium assembly behaviors not seen in uniform grafting.
conclusion: The work provides insights into designing polymer-grafted nanoparticles for controlled self-assembly, but is not directly related to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Wake-tail Effects In Two-dimensional Wave Refocusing
authors: Theodoros T. Koutserimpas

In even spatial dimensions, solutions of the wave equation violate Huygens' principle, producing a persistent wake tail inside the light cone rather than a sharply localized propagating front. method: The authors analyze the wave equation in two spatial dimensions, where Huygens' principle is violated, leading to a persistent wake tail that affects refocusing.

conclusion: The work provides insights into classical wave propagation but has no relevance to the user's research interests.

[Phys. Rev. E 113, 065103] Published Thu Jun 11, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies the resonance behavior of a gas microbubble near a spherical inclusion in a viscous fluid, with applications in medical ultrasound and cavitation.
motivation: Understanding bubble dynamics near inclusions is important for applications like targeted drug delivery and ultrasound imaging, but the paper does not connect to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.
method: An analytical model is developed for the frequency response of a bubble oscillating near a spherical inclusion, considering radial and nonspherical modes and different inclusion properties.
result: The model predicts resonance frequencies and damping rates as functions of inclusion size and mechanical properties.
conclusion: The work provides a theoretical framework for bubble-inclusion interactions but has no relevance to the user's research interests.

title: Humidity As A Critical Parameter For Predicting Breakdown Voltage In Submicrometer Electrode Gaps In Air
authors: B. Disson, N. Bonifaci, O. Lesaint, C. Poulain, R. Dussart, And S. Iseni

This experimental work reinvestigates the breakdown voltage in air for electrode gaps ranging from [MATH] to [MATH]. Rarely addressed in the literature of the field, a special focus is placed on varying the gas humidity and its direct impact on the breakdown vo…


[Phys. Rev. E 113, 065207] Published Thu Jun 11, 2026.
tldr: This paper experimentally studies the effect of humidity on breakdown voltage in submicrometer electrode gaps in air.
motivation: Understanding breakdown in small gaps is important for microelectronics and MEMS, but the role of humidity is often overlooked.
method: Experimental measurements of breakdown voltage in air for electrode gaps from 0.5 to 10 μm at controlled humidity levels.
result: Humidity significantly affects breakdown voltage, with higher humidity reducing the breakdown voltage.
conclusion: Humidity must be considered as a critical parameter for predicting breakdown in submicrometer gaps.

title: Linear Rayleigh-Taylor Instability With Foams

[Phys. Rev. E 113, 065409] Published Thu Jun 11, 2026.
tldr: This paper analyzes the linear phase of the Rayleigh-Taylor instability in the presence of a foam, relevant to inertial confinement fusion.
motivation: Understanding the effect of foams on the Rayleigh-Taylor instability is important for improving inertial confinement fusion designs.

conclusion: Foams can mitigate the Rayleigh-Taylor instability in inertial confinement fusion, potentially improving implosion performance.

title: Compressibility Control On Gas-liquid-grain Displacement Dynamics
authors: Feihu Ke And Chung-Yee Kwok

This study probes how gas compression governs the morphodynamics of gas-liquid-grain displacement in confined granular systems, a process vital to many applications like air sparging and carbon sequestration. result: Facilitating compression yields effects on displacement patterns.

title: Leidenfrost Hydrogels: Elastic Surface-wave Instability And Sustained Bouncing
authors: Nathan C. J. Coombs, Peter Lewin-Jones, Mykyta V. Chubynsky, And James E. Sprittles
abstract:

title: When Surface Dynamics Fakes Symmetry: Oxygen On Rh(100) Revisited
authors: Lutz Hammer, Tilman Kißlinger, Margareta Wagner, Reinhard B. Neder, Michael Schmid, Ulrike Diebold, And M. Alexander Schneider
abstract:
Author(s): Lutz Hammer, Tilman Kißlinger, Margareta Wagner, Reinhard B. Neder, Michael Schmid, Ulrike Diebold, and M. Alexander Schneider

Heating a long-range ordered adsorbate phase beyond its stability temperature does not necessarily result in a disordered phase; it can also break up into heavily fluctuating ordered domains. Temporal and/or spatial averaging over these fluctuations may give the impression of both a wrong periodicit…


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 023296] Published Mon Jun 15, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies oxygen adsorption on Rh(100) surface, revealing that fluctuating ordered domains can mimic a wrong surface symmetry under thermal averaging.
motivation: To understand the behavior of adsorbate phases beyond their stability temperature and to explain apparent symmetry changes observed in surface experiments.

result: Heating the ordered phase leads to heavily fluctuating domains that, upon averaging, give the false impression of a different periodicity and symmetry.

title: Commissioning And Full Realization Of A Collinear Resonance Ionization Spectroscopy Setup At Beijing Radioactive Ion-beam Facility
authors: W. C. Mei et Al.
